**Authors:** Allison F. Gilmour, Brendan Bartanen, Elizabeth Bettini, Li Feng, Jamie Klinenberg, Loretta Mason-Williams, Christopher Redding, LaRon A. Scott, and Roddy Theobald
**Review Date:** 2026-09-02

### Overall Assessment: Solid Contribution

This paper is the first to run one harmonized measurement protocol — common special-education-teacher (SET) identification rules, CEDS-aligned variable definitions, within-state quartiles, and identical linear probability models — across seven state longitudinal data systems (Hawaii, Indiana, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, Washington; 2017–18 to 2022–23), and the field should treat it as the default reference for two things: that SET workforce challenges differ substantially in kind and magnitude across states, and that within any state the teachers who leave, switch to general education, or move schools are disproportionately novices and SETs without full special education certification. Those within-state, teacher-level results are the paper's firmest ground — fully certified SETs are less likely to leave teaching in all seven states (from 2.4 points in Virginia to 18.8 in Texas), novices turn over more on nearly every margin in nearly every state, special education schools employ fewer fully certified SETs in every state (6.7 to 73.5 points), and charter schools in the four states with substantial charter sectors staff more novices and fewer certified SETs and lose more of them — and the paper's central interpretive claim, that descriptive turnover gaps between high- and low-poverty schools largely reflect which teachers are sorted into those schools rather than school context per se, survives every methodological objection raised here and would only strengthen under correct inference. Readers should be more careful with the cross-state half of the paper. States identify SETs with different instruments (an indicator, assignment codes, student population served, classroom setting, a funding code), attrition means leaving the state's public-school file, Pennsylvania's intermediate-unit SETs and all district-office SETs are excluded, and Indiana's panel ends in 2019–20; so cross-state rankings of levels — SET share of the workforce, switching rates, attrition rates — and the very large Indiana and Texas certification–switching coefficients carry a definitional component the authors themselves flag. No cross-state difference is formally tested, standard errors are clustered by teacher although most predictors vary at the school or district level, and the school- and district-demographic coefficients (district percent English learners above all) should be discounted accordingly. Two further cautions concern the prose rather than the evidence: several of the summary sentences that generalize across states are wrong against the paper's own tables (a sign reversal for Texas SETs of color moving schools, misidentified exception states, a high-school switching claim contradicted in four states, a Discussion sentence about Pennsylvania and Indiana that reverses Table 2), the Figure 3 and Figure 5 captions mislabel what the panels show, the Discussion's "turnover of nearly half the workforce" has no counterpart in the reported statewide maximum of 35.9%, and the Conclusion's "likely driven by" upgrades a prose-only model-building exercise into a mechanism. Cite the paper for its within-state associations, its school-type findings, and the existence and rough scale of cross-state heterogeneity; quote numbers from Tables 1–6 rather than from the text; and read the companion methods paper (Gilmour et al., 2026, Teacher Education and Special Education) before leaning on any cross-state comparison of levels.

#### Key Strengths

- **Harmonized seven-state infrastructure that did not previously exist.** Prior SET workforce evidence came from national survey snapshots or single-state SLDS studies with incompatible definitions; this study holds the SET-identification rule (≥50% of assignments or ≥0.50 FTE), variable construction, quartile scheme, and model specification fixed across seven states, with a dated preregistration, an itemized deviations section, full regression output and code on OSF, a public data explorer, and a companion paper on measurement sensitivity. The infrastructure is the contribution most likely to still matter in a decade.
- **Robust within-state teacher-level findings.** Full certification is negatively associated with attrition in every state (Table 4), novices have higher attrition, switching, and moving in nearly every state (Tables 4–6), and — because these attributes vary within school — teacher-level clustering is roughly the right inference for them. These are the estimates least exposed to the paper's cross-state comparability problems.
- **The distribution–stability entanglement is well supported and methodologically safe.** Descriptive turnover gaps by school poverty and student race largely disappear once novice status and certification enter the models (school % FRPL is unrelated to attrition in every state in Table 4), and the paper reads this correctly as evidence that less-experienced, uncertified SETs are sorted into schools serving marginalized students. Correct clustering would push the residual school and district coefficients further toward zero, not away.
- **Several substantive facts new to the SET literature.** Special education schools have lower full-certification rates in all seven states (contradicting prior SASS-based work, which the authors flag rather than bury); turnover in those schools is sharply heterogeneous across states (lower in MA/TX/WA, 21.4 points higher attrition in VA); switching to general education is quantified as a major and state-varying outflow; the SET-versus-general-educator attrition gap is modest (1.2–5.5 points) and absent in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania; and the certification and novice coefficients themselves vary several-fold across states.
- **Unusual candor about the limits of its own comparisons.** The Discussion names Indiana's and Texas's SET-identification rules as likely inflators of those states' switching rates and low SET shares, the Limitations concede that seemingly comparable variables "were not comparable in practice," missingness is quantified (12.3% of school-years and 71.9% of district-years missing a covariate; 18.8% of Virginia SETs missing race), and the ethnoracial aggregation is framed and honored consistently.

#### Key Concerns

- **Cross-state comparisons of levels are entangled with definitions and sample construction.** SETs are identified by different instruments in each state; attrition means exit from the state's public-school file (so out-of-state moves, private schools, district-office promotions, and Pennsylvania's excluded intermediate units all count as leaving); Indiana's analytic window is 2017–18 to 2019–20 only; and novice status is inferred from first appearance in the panel. The paper's headline heterogeneity is never formally tested — seven separate regressions are compared by which cells carry stars, across many hundreds of coefficients with no multiplicity adjustment — so differential significance across states is not evidence that states differ.
- **Inference on school- and district-level predictors is overstated.** Standard errors are clustered by teacher (a handful of observations each) while school %FRPL, %Black, %Hispanic, school type, urbanicity, and every district variable are constant within school-year or district-year cells containing many SETs. A Moulton-type correction would remove many of the stars on district coefficients in Tables 1–6. District % English learners is additionally carried forward from stale years and changes source mid-panel, and produces implausible magnitudes (e.g., 0.123 per SD on novice status in Virginia, −0.123 on switching in Texas). One Table 4 cell (Pennsylvania district %EL, 0.0067 with SE 0.0044) is starred at p<.05 with t≈1.5.
- **Text–table disagreements cluster in exactly the sentences readers will quote.** "SETs of color moved schools at a higher rate than White teachers only in Texas" — Table 6's Texas cell is −0.0040*. "All states except Washington" for SETs of color — Massachusetts is equally null in Tables 4–6. "All states except Hawaii" for school level — Hawaii is significant in all three tables; Indiana is the null state. "High school SETs switched … or moved" less — switching is significantly higher in HI, MA, TX, VA (Table 5). The Discussion's claim that Pennsylvania SETs of color work in higher-FRPL schools reverses Table 2 (−0.0048*). Figure 3's caption and text swap the panels; Figure 5's caption says "attrition" but every number drawn from it is total turnover.
- **Two quotable claims outrun the reported evidence.** "Turnover of nearly half the workforce (which we found in one state …)" has no counterpart in the article; the highest statewide total turnover reported is Texas at 35.9%, and total turnover includes within-state school moves. The Conclusion's "higher turnover in schools serving more marginalized student populations was likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs" is a mediation claim resting on a model-building exercise described in one sentence of prose with no table, while switching and moving retain positive school-poverty associations in four states (Tables 5–6).
- **Reporting and transparency gaps limit verification.** No descriptive-statistics table (every level and trend lives only in Figures 1–5); no outcome means, R², or school/district counts; advanced-degree and gender models and the model-building results exist only on OSF or in prose; Ns differ non-monotonically across Tables 4–6 within state (Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361), leaving the switching and moving estimands ambiguous; it is unstated whether the 1/(number of schools) weights enter the regressions; and there is no data availability statement or described access pathway for the seven state agreements. The literature review is also thin on adjacent work that changes interpretation — targeted-compensation causal studies, teacher sorting, charter certification exemptions, community-eligibility effects on FRPL, and evidence that turnover is not uniformly harmful.

#### What to Rely On

- **Within-state associations between teacher attributes and turnover.** Fully certified SETs are less likely to leave teaching in all seven states (Table 4: −2.4 points in Virginia to −18.8 in Texas) and less likely to switch to general education in six (Table 5); novices are more likely to leave (1.9 points in Pennsylvania to 10.1 in Hawaii; not in Texas), switch (1.6–4.5 points), and move (1.2–6.9 points). These are the paper's most durable estimates.
- **Special education schools employ fewer fully certified SETs than traditional schools in every state** (Table 3: 6.7 points in Texas to 73.5 in Hawaii). A within-state, within-year contrast that holds under seven different SET-identification rules, and a genuine correction to prior SASS-based findings.
- **The charter-sector pattern, as direction, in states with substantial charter sectors (IN, MA, PA, TX):** more novices (Table 1: 22.6–29.3 points), fewer fully certified SETs (Table 3), and higher attrition (Table 4: 7.4–11.0 points). Consistent with the general-education charter literature.
- **Teacher characteristics dominate school and district demographics in turnover models.** School % FRPL is not associated with attrition in any state once teacher attributes are controlled (Table 4), and school/district demographic coefficients are on the order of 0.5–1.5 points per SD. The descriptive turnover gaps by school poverty and race (Figure 5) largely reflect which SETs are sorted into those schools — the paper's best-supported interpretive claim.
- **The existence and rough scale of cross-state heterogeneity, as a pattern.** Average total turnover of 35.9% in Texas versus 16.8% in Pennsylvania; switching a large share of turnover in Indiana, Massachusetts, and Texas; average attrition of 6.1% in Pennsylvania versus 16.7% in Virginia; SET workforces 88–95% White in PA/MA/IN/WA versus 27–67% teachers of color in VA/TX/HI. Rely on the large, directionally consistent contrasts, not on fine differences.
- **SET attrition exceeds general-educator attrition in most but not all states, and by modest margins** (1.2 points in Texas to 5.5 in Virginia; not in Massachusetts or Pennsylvania, Figure 3). A useful corrective to the blanket claim that SETs leave at much higher rates.
- **The harmonized definitions themselves** (CEDS-aligned novice, full certification, and four-way turnover coding; the ≥50%/≥0.50 FTE SET rule; within-state quartiles) as a template for cross-state SET workforce research, with the companion Gilmour et al. (2026, TESE) paper as the measurement reference.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- **"Turnover of nearly half the workforce … in one state."** The highest statewide total turnover the article reports is 35.9% (Texas), and total turnover counts within-state school moves as turnover; quote 35.9% (TX) and 16.8% (PA) instead, and say what they include.
- **The Conclusion's "likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs."** No mediation or decomposition analysis is presented; the supporting model-building lives in one prose sentence; and the compositional story is clean only for attrition — switching and moving retain school-poverty associations in four states. The Discussion's "may be due to" is the supportable version.
- **Cross-state rankings of levels — SET share of the workforce (8.6% IN to 18.4% HI), certification rates, switching rates, attrition rates.** Each state identifies SETs with a different instrument, attrition includes out-of-state and private-school exits and district-office moves, and Pennsylvania's intermediate-unit SETs are excluded; the authors themselves attribute Indiana's and Texas's low SET shares and high switching to identification rules.
- **The Indiana and Texas certification–switching coefficients (Table 5: −0.403 and −0.311 versus −0.04 to −0.09 elsewhere) and the Texas policy inference built on them.** These are the two states whose SET definitions (classroom setting; student population served) the authors flag as likely to inflate switching, and certification is endogenous to intent to stay. Do not read certification as a causal retention lever.
- **Any "significant in state X but not state Y" contrast.** Cross-state differences are never formally tested, there is no multiplicity adjustment across roughly a thousand coefficients, and teacher-level clustering understates SEs on school/district regressors. Only very large contrasts (e.g., −18.8 vs. −2.4 on certification–attrition) should be treated as established heterogeneity.
- **School- and district-level demographic coefficients in Tables 1–6, especially district % English learners.** Clustered at the wrong level, built from covariates carried forward across 71.9% of district-years, and (for %EL) drawn from two sources across the panel; several magnitudes are implausible. Treat as suggestive.
- **Specific summary sentences that contradict the tables.** Texas SETs of color move schools at a *lower* rate (Table 6, −0.0040*); Massachusetts, not only Washington, shows no SET-of-color stability differences; Indiana, not Hawaii, is the state with no school-level stability associations; high-school SETs switch *more* in HI, MA, TX, VA (Table 5); Pennsylvania SETs of color are *less* likely to work in high-FRPL schools (Table 2). Verify any across-state quantifier against the table row before repeating it.
- **Figure 3 and Figure 5 as captioned.** Caption and text disagree on which Figure 3 panel is attrition and which is certification; Figure 5's caption says "attrition distribution" but the text draws total-turnover figures from it. Read the axis labels, not the captions.
- **Indiana estimates and any pandemic-era trend claim that includes Indiana.** Indiana's analytic sample runs 2017–18 to 2019–20 only — roughly two transitions, entirely pre-COVID — while the other six states span 2017–18 to 2022–23.
- **Charter-school magnitudes for Washington (0.405 on novice status; 0.258 on attrition) and Virginia (insignificant throughout), and the switching/moving estimands in Tables 5–6.** Tiny charter sectors and unreported school counts sit behind the WA/VA cells; school type was added after preregistration; and the non-monotonic Ns across Tables 4–6 leave unclear whether switching and moving are estimated conditional on not leaving.
- **The supplemental-analysis sentence that hazard models show "SETs of color or novice SETs had higher probabilities of attrition" in many states.** The main Table 4 shows SETs of color with significantly *lower* attrition in Hawaii and Texas and higher in only Indiana and Pennsylvania; the hazard results are OSF-only and cover early-career SETs.
- **The literature-review generalizations that the paper's own results qualify** — that SET turnover is "consistently higher" than other teachers' (not in MA/PA), that inequities in SET qualifications "may have closed" (novices concentrate in high-FRPL schools in PA/VA/TX), and the "15% of SETs leave their schools annually" figure (the paper's own total turnover runs 16.8–35.9%). Check the cited sources before repeating.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The design — harmonize seven state longitudinal data systems, then run the same descriptive and linear-probability analyses separately within each state — is well matched to a descriptive question about workforce composition, distribution, and stability, and the execution is unusually transparent (preregistration, OSF code, an explicit companion paper on measurement sensitivity, a candid limitations section). The weak point is inference and cross-state comparability: standard errors are clustered by teacher while the school- and district-level predictors that generate many of the reported stars are constant within school-year and district-year, and the paper's headline claim of cross-state variation is never formally tested and is partly confounded with documented differences in how each state identifies special education teachers. Within-state associations between teacher attributes and turnover are solid; cross-state comparisons of levels and magnitudes are the fragile part.

**Strengths:**

- The core methodological contribution is real and correctly executed: rather than comparing published estimates from seven separately designed single-state studies, the authors applied one variable-construction protocol and one model specification to seven SLDSs. That removes analyst degrees of freedom as an explanation for cross-state differences, which is exactly the gap the paper identifies (Gilmour et al., 2025) and something no prior study delivers.
- Unusual transparency for a descriptive workforce paper: preregistration with the Center for Open Science (October 2024), deviations from preregistration reported explicitly and with reasons (discrete-time hazard models replaced by LPMs; experience constructed from the panel), full regression output and supplemental analyses posted to OSF, and a separate companion paper (Gilmour et al., 2026) devoted to the sensitivity of results to SET-identification and multi-school-assignment rules.
- Sensible modeling choices for the question asked. LPMs are defensible here (outcomes are not rare; coefficients are directly readable in percentage points; logistic re-estimation is reported as substantively unchanged), and within-state standardization of continuous school/district variables plus within-state quartiles for the descriptive cuts is the right framing for a labor-market question where teachers choose among options inside one state.
- The paper's central interpretive move is methodologically correct and self-aware. The authors observe that descriptive turnover gaps by school poverty and student race largely disappear once teacher characteristics enter Equation (2), and correctly read this as evidence that distribution and stability are entangled — the schools with higher turnover are the schools staffed with novice and uncertified SETs — rather than claiming school demographics do not matter. They also note the associations between SET-of-color status and turnover in IN and PA fall by roughly half once school characteristics are added.
- Limitations are stated candidly and several are quantified rather than gestured at: 12.3% of school-years and 71.9% of district-years missing at least one CCD variable, 18.8% of Virginia SETs missing race/ethnicity, the acknowledgment that identifying SETs by setting (IN) or student population served (TX) may conflate SETs with general educators and inflate switching rates in exactly those states.
- Within-state benchmarking against general education teachers on the two most policy-salient measures (full certification and attrition, Figure 3) partly rescues quantities — like certification rates — that are otherwise not comparable across states with different licensure architectures.

**Weaknesses:**

- Standard errors are clustered by teacher, but the school and district predictors that carry much of the paper's argument are constant within school-year and district-year cells containing many teachers. Teacher clustering absorbs within-teacher serial correlation across roughly 2-5 observations; it does nothing about correlated residuals among the hundreds of SETs in the same district. The resulting Moulton-type understatement is modest for school-level variables and potentially severe for district-level ones, so a large share of the stars in Tables 1-6 on school and district variables are not trustworthy at face value.
- The paper's headline claim — that challenges vary across states — is never formally tested. Seven separate regressions are estimated and their coefficients and significance stars are compared narratively ("significant in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Texas but not elsewhere"). With well over a thousand coefficients evaluated at p <= .05 and no multiplicity adjustment, and with the SE problem above, patterns of which states cross the threshold are a weak basis for concluding heterogeneity.
- LPM coefficients are compared across states in raw percentage points even though base rates differ by a factor of three or more (average attrition of 6.1% in Pennsylvania vs. 16.7% in Virginia; total turnover of 16.8% in PA vs. 35.9% in TX). The scope for a large absolute gap is mechanically larger where the outcome is more common, so statements like "the association is much larger in Texas than Virginia" partly restate differences in base rates. The tables report no outcome means, no R-squared, and no counts of unique teachers, schools, or districts, so a reader cannot do the normalization or judge how many clusters underlie any estimate.
- "Novice" and "attrition" are both constructed from presence in the panel — first appearance and last appearance, respectively — which builds in a mechanical component to the novice-turnover association. Any single-year appearance (an out-of-state hire who leaves, a long-term substitute, a re-entrant, an identifier-linkage failure) is coded both novice and attriter. The authors acknowledge that re-entrants inflate the novice count; the more consequential point is that the inflation is concentrated among short spells and therefore biases the novice coefficient in Tables 4-6 upward, by an amount that may vary with each state's identifier quality.
- Attrition means leaving the state's public-school teaching data, so it pools genuine exits from teaching with out-of-state moves, moves to private schools, and moves into non-teaching roles. Because the sample also excludes SETs employed by intermediate units and other non-district entities and SETs in district-level roles, a promotion into a district office is coded as attrition. Both features vary systematically with state geography and administrative structure (Pennsylvania's intermediate units, Hawaii's single district and island geography, Texas's size), which contaminates precisely the cross-state level comparisons the paper foregrounds.
- Cross-state comparability of the SET population itself is limited by design: Hawaii uses a direct indicator; MA, PA, and VA use assignment codes; TX uses student population served; IN uses instructional setting; WA uses a special education funding code. The authors flag that the IN and TX definitions may inflate switching. That caution should be read as load-bearing: the two states with the widest definitions produce full-certification coefficients on switching of -0.403 (IN) and -0.311 (TX) in Table 5, an order of magnitude larger than HI (-0.037), WA (-0.042), PA (-0.046), or MA (-0.087), which is what one would expect if year-to-year changes in caseload or setting are being read as career changes.
- Missing CCD covariates are filled by carrying forward the most recent non-missing value, with 71.9% of district-years missing at least one variable. This is defensible triage but leaves the district-level covariates — English learner share in particular, whose source changes mid-panel from CCD to Ed Data Express for 2020-21 and 2021-22 — measured with substantial error. The district %EL coefficients are correspondingly erratic and implausibly large in places (0.123 per SD on novice status in VA, Table 1; -0.103 on full certification in VA, Table 3; -0.123 on switching in TX, Table 5).
- FRPL is used to define the poverty quartiles behind Figure 5 and as a standardized continuous control, but community eligibility has made school-level FRPL a state- and year-varying proxy for poverty. Only Massachusetts is corrected (using DESE economic disadvantage). This bears directly on one of the paper's most quoted contrasts — a 10.1 pp high- versus low-poverty turnover gap in Pennsylvania versus 1.4 pp in Texas — since compression of the FRPL measure in states with widespread CEP adoption would attenuate the gradient for reasons having nothing to do with teacher labor markets.
- Estimation samples for the three turnover outcomes differ within state in a way the text never explains. Massachusetts has 50,627 observations for attrition (Table 4), 52,605 for switching (Table 5), and 47,995 for moving (Table 6); Indiana has 12,507 / 13,822 / 12,892; Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361. If the outcomes are mutually exclusive categories defined on a common base-year sample, the denominators should match. Whether this reflects outcome-specific missingness or estimation of each turnover type against stayers only (dropping the other categories) changes how the coefficients should be read, and readers cannot tell from the article.
- There are no school or district fixed effects anywhere, so every 'all else equal' school and district estimate is a between-school comparison conditioned on a short list of CCD covariates. This is appropriate to a descriptive aim, but it means the school-type results absorb all unobserved differences in schools and in teacher sorting. In Tables 4-6 the school and district coefficients are additionally conditioned on novice status and certification — the very channel the paper argues transmits inequity — so their near-zero values are partly by construction, not evidence that school context is irrelevant. The Discussion mostly handles this correctly but slides toward causal-sounding policy language in places, particularly on charter schools.
- Of the five composition outcomes named in Research Question 1, only three (novice, SET of color, full certification) appear as main-text tables. Advanced degree and gender models are discussed in the results narrative but live only on OSF, and advanced degree is unavailable in HI and IN at all. Virginia's SET-of-color models drop the 18.8% with missing race data (N = 87,217 in Table 2 vs. 108,623 in Tables 1 and 3), so if race reporting is non-random across Virginia districts, the Virginia ethnoracial distribution results are the least reliable in the paper.
- Seven states selected by data-sharing feasibility, one of which is a single-district state. This is not a probability sample of states and the paper does not claim otherwise, but the set omits California, New York, Florida, Illinois, and the Deep South, and over-represents states with mature SLDS research partnerships.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Trust the teacher-level coefficients in Tables 4-6 and discount the school- and district-level ones. Novice status, full certification, and SET-of-color status vary within school, so teacher clustering is roughly the right level for them, and the magnitudes are large: novices are 1.9 pp (PA) to 10.1 pp (HI) more likely to leave and 1.2-6.9 pp more likely to move; fully certified SETs are less likely to leave in every one of the seven states. Those are the paper's most durable results.
- Apply a mental correction factor to district-level estimates before believing any of them. Clustering by teacher ignores the correlation among the hundreds of SETs sharing a district-year value of a district regressor. As an illustration, the PA district %Black coefficient on novice status in Table 1 is 0.0208 (SE 0.0028), a t of about 7.4; a Moulton inflation of 4-5, which is not extreme for clusters of this size, would put it near conventional insignificance. Treat district %FRPL, %Hispanic, %Black, %EL, and district enrollment throughout Tables 1-6 as suggestive at best. School-level demographic coefficients are less affected but still need discounting, and most are already tiny (the authors put them at 0.5-1.5 pp per SD).
- Do not read 'significant in state X but not state Y' as evidence that the states differ. No test of equality across states is reported anywhere, and with this many coefficients and no multiplicity adjustment, differential significance is largely noise plus the SE problem. Where you want a heterogeneity claim, rely on the differences that are large and directionally consistent across many coefficients — total turnover of 35.9% in TX versus 16.8% in PA, or the concentration of switching in IN, MA, and TX — not on star patterns in individual rows.
- Treat the switching results for Indiana and Texas as the most likely artifacts in the paper. Those two states identify SETs by instructional setting and by student population served, and the authors themselves warn this may inflate switching. The corresponding full-certification coefficients in Table 5 (IN -0.403, TX -0.311) are 4-10 times those in states using assignment codes or indicators, which is what an identification artifact would look like. The recommendation that Massachusetts and Indiana need policy levers to make SET work more appealing relative to general education rests substantially on this quantity, as does the framing of Texas HB 2.
- Read cross-state differences in attrition levels as differences in exit-from-the-state's-teaching-file, not exit from teaching. Out-of-state moves, private-school moves, promotions into district-level roles, and moves to intermediate units all count as attrition, and their prevalence varies with state size, geography, and administrative structure. The within-state comparison to general education teachers (Figure 3) is the more defensible reading of each state's attrition number.
- Take the school-type findings as the paper's most robust structural result, with two caveats. Special education schools have lower predicted probabilities of full certification in all seven states (6.7 pp in TX to 73.5 pp in HI, Table 3), and charter schools employ more novices and fewer fully certified SETs and have higher attrition in most states with a charter sector. But the magnitudes at the extremes rest on very small numbers of schools that the tables never report — Virginia has a handful of charter schools (its charter coefficients are insignificant throughout) and Washington's charter sector is tiny yet produces the largest coefficients in the table (0.405 on novice, 0.258 on attrition). Rely on the direction, which holds across IN, MA, PA, and TX where the sectors are substantial; do not rely on the WA or VA magnitudes.
- Before comparing coefficient magnitudes across states, divide by each state's base rate. A 1.9 pp novice-attrition gap on Pennsylvania's 6.1% attrition base is proportionally larger than it looks next to Virginia's 2.9 pp on a 16.7% base. Because Tables 1-6 report no outcome means, this normalization requires reading Figures 3-5 or the supplement.
- Read the paper's central negative finding as robust and, if anything, understated. The claim that school and district demographic characteristics are only weakly and inconsistently associated with turnover once teacher characteristics are controlled survives the SE problem — proper clustering would push those coefficients further toward insignificance, not away. The corollary conclusion, that higher turnover in schools serving marginalized students is driven mainly by the inequitable distribution of novice and uncertified SETs into those schools, is the paper's best-supported substantive claim.
- Discount the district %English-learner coefficients heavily wherever they appear. The variable is missing in a large share of district-years, carried forward, and drawn from a different source (Ed Data Express) for 2020-21 and 2021-22, and it produces some of the largest and least stable coefficients in the paper (VA 0.123 on novice, VA -0.103 on certification, TX -0.123 on switching).
- Treat Virginia's SET-of-color distribution results (Table 2) as the weakest cell in the design: nearly 20% of Virginia SETs lack race data and those observations are dropped from that model. Virginia's turnover models handle missingness with an indicator instead, so the two are not doing the same thing.
- Note that Indiana's analytic window is 2017-18 to 2019-20, not 2017-18 to 2022-23. Indiana's turnover estimates rest on roughly two year-to-year transitions ending at the onset of the pandemic, so Indiana should be excluded from any reading of the post-COVID trend the paper describes (attrition dipping in 2019-20, rising for two years, then stabilizing) and its estimates carry far less temporal averaging than the other six states.
- If you plan to build on a specific coefficient, go to the OSF site (https://osf.io/qkpnz/) first. The full regression output, the intraclass correlations, the descriptive t-tests, the advanced-degree and gender models, the logistic and discrete-time hazard robustness checks, and the state-by-state SET-identification and quartile documentation all live there rather than in the article, and several of them are what you would need to judge whether a particular estimate is solid.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Design fit. The research questions are explicitly descriptive — how do composition, distribution, and stability of the special education teacher workforce vary across states, within states, and over time — and the design matches. There is no causal claim to identify, no treatment, and no attempt to manufacture one. What the paper is really doing methodologically is harmonization: taking seven state longitudinal data systems that use incompatible conventions and forcing one variable-construction protocol and one specification onto all of them, so that observed differences across states cannot be attributed to differences in how seven separate research teams defined 'novice' or 'turnover.' That is a genuine and non-trivial contribution, and it is the right response to the problem the authors themselves diagnosed in Gilmour et al. (2025). The transparency infrastructure around it — preregistration, posted code, an itemized list of deviations from the preregistration, and a separate companion paper devoted to measurement sensitivity — is well above the norm for descriptive workforce research.

Inference is the weakest link. Both Equation (1) and Equation (2) cluster standard errors by SET, justified in the text as accounting for correlation in outcomes for the same teacher over time. That justification is correct as far as it goes, but it addresses the wrong dimension for most of what the tables report. Each teacher contributes only a handful of observations, so teacher clustering is close to heteroskedasticity-robust inference. Meanwhile the regressors that generate a large share of the reported stars — school %FRPL, school %Hispanic, school %Black, charter and special-education-school indicators, urbanicity, district enrollment, district %FRPL, district %Black, district %EL — are constant within school-year or district-year cells containing many teachers. With residual correlation among teachers in the same school or district, the Moulton correction factor scales with the number of observations per cluster. In Texas, 285,766 observations across roughly 1,200 districts is on the order of 240 observations per district-cluster; Pennsylvania is similar. Even modest within-cluster residual correlation produces inflation factors of three or more for district-level regressors, and perhaps a factor of two for school-level ones. Concretely: the Pennsylvania district %Black coefficient on novice status in Table 1 is 0.0208 with a reported SE of 0.0028, a t-statistic near 7.4, which survives a factor of three but not a factor of five. Many of the district coefficients in Tables 1-6 have t-statistics between 2 and 4 and would not survive. The practical implication is asymmetric and worth stating precisely: this problem attacks the paper's affirmative claims about where SETs are distributed and where they leave, while leaving its central negative claim untouched. The finding that school and district characteristics are inconsistently and weakly related to turnover once teacher attributes are controlled would only become stronger under correct clustering.

Compounding this, the paper compares seven separately estimated models with well over a thousand coefficients evaluated at p <= .05 with no multiplicity adjustment, and it never formally tests whether any coefficient differs across states. The entire heterogeneity argument — the paper's headline — is conducted by narrating which states show stars. Sentences of the form 'in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Texas, SETs in schools with higher percentages of students eligible for FRPL were more likely to be novices' describe which of seven independent draws crossed a threshold, not established cross-state differences. Where cross-state differences are large and consistent across many coefficients at once — total turnover of 35.9% in Texas versus 16.8% in Pennsylvania, the concentration of turnover in switching in IN/MA/TX, the near-universality of the special-education-school certification penalty — the claim stands on its face. Where it rests on a single row flipping sign or losing significance, it should not be relied upon.

Measurement is the other place a careful reader should slow down. Three constructions deserve scrutiny. First, SET identification differs fundamentally across the seven states: a direct indicator in Hawaii, assignment codes in MA/PA/VA, student population served in Texas, instructional setting in Indiana, and a special education funding code in Washington. The authors flag in the Discussion that the Texas and Indiana approaches may conflate SETs with general educators serving students with disabilities and may have inflated switching rates in those states. That caution is more load-bearing than its placement suggests. In Table 5, the full-certification coefficient on switching is -0.403 in Indiana and -0.311 in Texas, against -0.037 (HI), -0.042 (WA), -0.046 (PA), and -0.087 (MA). It is difficult to read that pattern as substantive rather than definitional: in a state where SET status depends on this year's caseload or setting, a teacher whose assignment shifts is recorded as switching to general education, and such teachers are disproportionately those without special education certification. It is also notable that Texas is the one state where novices are not more likely to leave teaching (-0.0015, n.s. in Table 4), the exception one would predict if Texas's SET population is diluted with general educators.

Second, 'novice' is defined by first appearance in the panel after a three-year washout (typically 2014-15 through 2016-17), and 'attrition' is defined by absence in the following year. Both are constructed from panel presence, which builds a mechanical component into their association. Re-entrants and out-of-state hires are coded novice, as the authors note; less discussed is that any observation arising from a short or fragmented spell — a one-year out-of-state hire, a long-term substitute, an identifier-linkage failure — is coded both novice and attriter simultaneously. The novice coefficients in Table 4 are large and almost certainly real (0.101 in Hawaii, 0.068 in Indiana, 0.048 in Washington), but part of their magnitude is definitional, and the cross-state spread in that magnitude may partly track differences in how stable each state's teacher identifiers are rather than differences in early-career retention. Indiana further deserves a flag: its analytic sample runs only 2017-18 to 2019-20, so its turnover estimates rest on roughly two transitions ending at the pandemic's onset (Table 4 N of 12,507 against 17,423 total), and Indiana cannot contribute to the paper's post-COVID trend narrative at all.

Third, attrition means leaving the state's public-school teaching records. It pools retirement, exit from education, moves out of state, moves to private schools, and promotion into non-teaching roles. Because the sample additionally excludes SETs employed by non-district entities such as Pennsylvania's intermediate units and SETs in district-level roles, moves into those positions are recorded as attrition. Each of these varies systematically with state geography and administrative structure. Cross-state comparisons of attrition levels — Pennsylvania at 6.1% versus Virginia at 16.7% — therefore blend real retention differences with differences in how much of each state's SET workforce sits outside the observed structures and how easy it is to cross a state line. The paper's within-state benchmark against general education teachers (Figure 3) is the sounder reading of any single state's number.

Covariate quality is a further constraint on the school and district results specifically. The authors report that 12.3% of school-year and 71.9% of district-year observations were missing at least one CCD variable, filled by carrying forward the most recent non-missing value. Carrying forward is a reasonable choice, but a 71.9% figure means the district covariate vector is substantially stale, and one component — district %English learners — additionally changes source mid-panel (CCD for 2017-18 to 2019-20, Ed Data Express for 2020-21 and 2021-22). Unsurprisingly, district %EL produces some of the largest and least stable estimates in the paper: 0.123 per standard deviation on novice status in Virginia (Table 1), -0.103 on full certification in Virginia (Table 3), -0.123 on switching in Texas (Table 5). Those magnitudes are not credible as substantive effects and should be read as measurement noise. FRPL raises a separate problem: community eligibility has made school-level FRPL a differentially compressed proxy for poverty across states and years, corrected here only for Massachusetts. Since FRPL defines the quartiles behind Figure 5, the widely quotable contrast between Pennsylvania's 10.1 pp high- versus low-poverty turnover gap and Texas's 1.4 pp gap has an entirely mechanical alternative explanation — that FRPL sorts Texas schools less finely — that the paper's own note about differing quartile cutpoints (Supplementary Appendix Table 3A) gestures at but does not resolve.

Two reporting gaps limit what a reader can independently verify. Tables 1-6 report only observation counts — no outcome means, no R-squared, and no counts of unique teachers, schools, or districts. Without base rates, the paper's repeated cross-state magnitude comparisons cannot be normalized (a 1.9 pp novice-attrition gap against Pennsylvania's 6.1% base is proportionally larger than Virginia's 2.9 pp against 16.7%). Without school counts, a reader cannot tell that Washington's charter coefficients (0.405 on novice, 0.258 on attrition) and Hawaii's special-education-school certification coefficient (-0.735) rest on very small numbers of schools, while Virginia's charter coefficients are insignificant throughout precisely because Virginia has almost no charter sector. Separately, the estimation samples for the three turnover outcomes differ within state in a way the text does not explain: Massachusetts has 50,627 / 52,605 / 47,995 observations across Tables 4, 5, and 6, Indiana 12,507 / 13,822 / 12,892, Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361. If the four turnover categories are mutually exclusive and drawn from one base-year sample, the denominators should be identical. Whether this reflects outcome-specific missingness or estimation of each turnover type against stayers only — which would make the coefficients conditional rather than unconditional probabilities and would mean Tables 4-6 do not decompose total turnover — materially changes interpretation, and the article does not say.

Finally, deviations from the preregistration are reported honestly and the substitutions are defensible, but readers should note their direction. Discrete-time hazard models were replaced by LPMs because following teachers over time would have dropped many observations and because experience data were unreliable in some states; experience was recoded from panel presence for the same reason. Both changes trade a design that models spells for one that pools teacher-years, which is more forgiving of exactly the data problems the paper faces. The hazard results appear only in the supplement and are described as consistent, which is reassuring but not independently checkable from the article.

What to rely on. The within-state associations between teacher attributes and turnover are the paper's firmest ground: novices turn over more on every margin in nearly every state, and fully certified SETs are less likely to leave teaching in all seven states. The special-education-school certification penalty holds in all seven states despite seven different SET-identification rules, which is the kind of consistency that survives the measurement critique. The charter pattern — more novices, fewer certified SETs, higher attrition — is consistent across the four states with substantial charter sectors. And the paper's central interpretive claim, that within-state turnover gaps by school poverty and student race are largely accounted for by the unequal distribution of novice and uncertified SETs rather than by school context conditional on staffing, is both well supported and robust to the standard-error problem. What to treat cautiously: cross-state comparisons of levels (attrition, switching, share of workforce that is SET), which are entangled with definitional and structural differences the authors themselves document; the switching results for Indiana and Texas specifically; every district-level coefficient; the district %EL coefficients in particular; Virginia's ethnoracial distribution results; and any conclusion that rests on a single coefficient crossing p = .05 in some states but not others.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The literature review is compact, well-organized around the paper's three research questions, and covers the core special education teacher (SET) workforce literature competently, including one commendable acknowledgment that the paper's special-education-school findings contradict prior SASS-based work. But it is thin for a 40-page article (roughly 2.5 pages), unusually self-referential (close to half the reference list involves at least one coauthor), and it states several prior findings more flatly than those findings hold. Readers should treat it as an adequate map of the SET-specific subfield and a poor map of the adjacent economics-of-teacher-labor-markets, charter-sector, and poverty-measurement literatures that bear directly on how the results should be interpreted.

**Strengths:**

- Tight architecture: the review is organized as Composition / Distribution / Stability, exactly mirroring RQ1-RQ3 and the Results and Discussion sections. A reader can trace every empirical claim back to the paragraph that motivates it, which is rarer than it should be in descriptive workforce papers.
- The core justification for the study is real and well-evidenced. The paper correctly identifies that the existing quantitative base splits into (a) nationally representative survey snapshots (SASS/NTPS-based work such as Bettini, Nguyen et al. 2022; Bettini et al. 2025; Gilmour et al. 2023) and (b) single-state SLDS studies (Theobald et al. 2021), with the further problem that variable definitions differ across the latter (citing Gilmour, Feng & Theobald 2025). That diagnosis is accurate and is the strongest part of the positioning.
- It explicitly names a contradiction with prior work rather than burying it: the finding that SETs in special education schools mostly do not differ from those in traditional schools is flagged as 'in contrast to prior studies that used the Schools and Staffing Survey (Mason-Williams & Gagnon, 2017; Mason-Williams et al., 2017),' with the certification exception noted. Papers routinely fail to do this, and the discussion's willingness to sit with the disagreement is a genuine credibility marker.
- The Discussion also correctly aligns its own null-after-controls pattern with Pendola & Perrone (2025), showing the authors are tracking the closest contemporaneous work rather than ignoring it.
- The equity framing is grounded in the right foundational SET citations (Mason-Williams 2015; Fall & Billingsley 2008; Billingsley & Bettini 2019 for the turnover taxonomy of attrition/switching/moving), and the switching category in particular is defined against a real prior literature rather than invented.
- The paper is honest in its Limitations that it benchmarks against general education teachers for only two variables, which implicitly concedes that much of the comparative literature it invokes is doing more work than its own design can support.

**Weaknesses:**

- NOVELTY CLAIM IS OVERSTATED IN ITS FLAT FORM. The Introduction and RQ section assert 'the first cross-state study to longitudinally quantify the nature and magnitude of SET workforce challenges' and 'the first cross-state and with-in state analysis of the challenges facing the SET workforce.' The Discussion's version is more defensible ('the first ... comprehensive, longitudinal, cross-state evaluation of the composition, distribution, AND stability'). But the paper itself cites Pendola & Perrone (2025, AERA Open) for the proposition that 'the rate at which SETs leave varies greatly across states' - which means cross-state longitudinal quantification of SET stability already existed in the literature the paper cites. The honest claim is narrower and, in my view, more interesting: this is the first study to apply a single harmonized measurement protocol to seven states' SLDSs across all three constructs simultaneously.
- THE MEASUREMENT CONTRIBUTION IS PARADOXICALLY UNDERSOLD WHILE THE SUBSTANTIVE ONE IS OVERSOLD. The paper's real innovation is harmonization, yet the two companion papers that carry the measurement argument (Gilmour, Feng & Theobald 2025 RSE; Gilmour, Klinenberg et al. 2026 TESE) are cited only in passing ('reported elsewhere'). This matters because the Discussion concedes that the states with the lowest SET shares (Indiana, Texas) are exactly the states where SET identification may have conflated SETs with general educators - i.e., the sensitivity of the headline cross-state variation to identification choices lives in a companion paper the reader must go find.
- HEAVY SELF-CITATION IN A SMALL SUBFIELD. Of roughly 50 references, a large share involve at least one of the nine coauthors (Bettini x4, Gilmour x4, Mason-Williams x4, Theobald appears in six or seven entries counting the Goldhaber collaborations, Scott x2, Redding, Nguyen). SET workforce research genuinely is a small community, so this is not misconduct - but readers should understand that the 'state of knowledge' presented here is substantially this team's own prior work, and that independent corroboration for several framing claims is thin.
- ECONOMICS OF TEACHER COMPENSATION IS ABSENT, INCLUDING A COAUTHOR'S OWN DIRECTLY RELEVANT WORK. The paper ends by recommending 'differential compensation programs, such as Hawaii's,' citing only Theobald et al. (2025). The causal literature on targeted retention/recruitment incentives - Clotfelter, Glennie, Ladd & Vigdor (2008) on North Carolina; Springer, Swain & Rodriguez (2016) on Tennessee; and most pointedly Feng & Sass on Florida's incentives for hard-to-staff subjects including special education (Li Feng is a coauthor here) - is nowhere in the review. A reader who wants to know whether the paper's own policy recommendation works has to leave the paper to find out.
- THE 'SORTING, NOT DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT' MECHANISM IS PRESENTED AS MORE NOVEL THAN IT IS. The paper's central interpretive finding - that descriptive turnover gaps across high- and low-poverty schools largely disappear once SET characteristics are controlled, so the gaps reflect the inequitable *distribution* of novice/uncertified SETs - has a deep antecedent in the general-education sorting literature (Boyd, Lankford, Loeb & Wyckoff on preferences and the draw of home; Hanushek, Kain & Rivkin 2004 on why teachers leave urban districts; Clotfelter, Ladd & Vigdor on teacher-quality gaps). Only Kalogrides et al. (2013), Goldhaber et al. (2015), and Bruno et al. (2020) appear, and none in the Discussion where the mechanism is claimed.
- CHARTER-SECTOR LITERATURE IS ESSENTIALLY ONE CITATION, AND THE OBVIOUS MECHANICAL EXPLANATION GOES UNSTATED. The charter results are among the largest in the paper (22.6-40.5 pp higher probability that a SET is a novice; 7.4-25.8 pp higher attrition), and the entire supporting literature is Weis, Woo & Nguyen (2024). Missing: Stuit & Smith (2012) on charter teacher turnover, Torres (2016) on no-excuses attrition, and the charter special-education enrollment literature (Winters; Setren). Most importantly, the review never mentions that charter schools in many states are exempt or partially exempt from teacher certification requirements - a mechanical explanation for the certification and novice gaps that a reader will otherwise mistake for a working-conditions story.
- NO ENGAGEMENT WITH FRPL/COMMUNITY-ELIGIBILITY MEASUREMENT PROBLEMS. School %FRPL quartiles carry the paper's entire poverty-based equity analysis, over 2017-18 to 2022-23. That window brackets both the acceleration of the Community Eligibility Provision and the USDA's pandemic-era universal free meals (2020-21, 2021-22), which are known to distort FRPL levels and cross-state comparability (Fazlul, Koedel & Parsons 2023; Domina et al. 2018). The paper notes Massachusetts missingness and substitutes DESE economic-disadvantage data - showing awareness of a state-specific problem - but never cites or discusses the general measurement literature. Cross-state comparisons of the FRPL gradient should be read with that caveat that the paper does not supply.
- TEACHER-OF-COLOR RETENTION LITERATURE IS UNDER-ENGAGED RELATIVE TO THE FINDING. The paper finds SETs of color more likely to leave in Indiana and Pennsylvania, less likely in Hawaii and Texas, with the IN/PA associations halving once school characteristics are added. That attenuation pattern is the central finding of a literature the review does not cite: Ingersoll & May on the minority-teacher 'revolving door' being an organizational-conditions phenomenon, Achinstein et al. (2010, RER), Carver-Thomas & Darling-Hammond. Bettini, Cormier et al. (2022) and Kim & Cooc (2021) appear only in the Limitations.
- INTERSTATE MOBILITY IS NEVER ADDRESSED AS A THREAT TO THE CENTRAL 'ATTRITION' CONSTRUCT. Attrition is defined as absence from the state dataset in year t+1 and is therefore a composite of leaving teaching, moving to another state, and moving to private schools. The paper notes Indiana private-school placements and Hawaii's island geography anecdotally, but cites nothing on how much state-exit overstates true attrition. This matters most for interpreting the headline cross-state levels (Virginia 16.7% vs. Pennsylvania 6.1%), where geography and border density plausibly drive part of the spread.
- ALL TURNOVER IS TREATED AS HARMFUL, WITH NO ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF CONTRARY EVIDENCE. The Stability section cites Ronfeldt et al. (2013), Sorensen & Ladd (2020), Kaler et al. (2025), and Synar & Maiden (2012), all pointing one direction, and the Discussion asserts that turnover of nearly half the workforce 'is clearly unsustainable.' The literature showing turnover can be neutral or beneficial when low performers exit (Adnot, Dee, Katz & Wyckoff 2017 on DC; Hanushek, Rivkin & Schiman 2016 on the composition-vs-disruption decomposition) is absent. Since the paper explicitly does not observe SET effectiveness (its own final limitation), the normative framing outruns both its evidence and the evidence it cites.
- TWO SHORTAGE STATISTICS FROM TWO SOURCES ARE NEVER RECONCILED, AND NEITHER IS CAVEATED. The Introduction says '45 states report SET shortages (Learning Policy Institute, 2025)'; two paragraphs later, 'In 2021, 49 states listed special education as a shortage area (U.S. Department of Education, 2026).' Both derive from state self-designations under the federal Teacher Shortage Areas process, which states have administrative incentives to declare broadly because designation triggers loan-forgiveness eligibility. The review presents these as measures of shortage magnitude without noting they are not.
- REFERENCE LIST HAS REAL ERRORS. Goldhaber & Theobald (2023, CALDER Policy Brief 32-0223) appears TWICE with two different URLs, and the duplicate is interleaved into the Kaler et al. (2025) entry, leaving Kaler et al. with no publisher, no institution, and no URL at all - despite carrying a causal-sounding claim about SET turnover harming students with disabilities. The Gershenson et al. (2022) DOI is malformed as 'https://0.1257/pol.20190573' (should be https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20190573). Sorensen is spelled 'Sorenson' in text. Alphabetization breaks in the Gilmour and Goldhaber runs. There appear to be two separate Digest of Education Statistics entries (NCES 2023, table dt23_203.70; U.S. Department of Education 2023, table dt23_204.70), only one of which is cited in text. Von Hippel (2015) - the sole authority for the LPM-over-logit choice - is a Statistical Horizons blog post, not peer-reviewed.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE THIS PAPER FOR WHAT IT ACTUALLY ESTABLISHES: harmonized, seven-state, longitudinal administrative estimates of SET composition, distribution, and stability using a common protocol. Do NOT cite it as the first cross-state longitudinal evidence that SET turnover varies across states - the paper's own citation to Pendola & Perrone (2025, AERA Open) establishes that predecessor, and that is where the priority for cross-state SET turnover variation belongs. For the SET-identification and multi-school-assignment sensitivity that underwrites all of these numbers, cite the companions: Gilmour, Feng & Theobald (2025, Remedial and Special Education 46(2)) and Gilmour, Klinenberg, Bettini, Mason-Williams & Theobald (2026, Teacher Education and Special Education 49(1)).
- VERIFY BEFORE REPEATING - the Goldhaber, Theobald & Fumia (2022) numbers. The paper attributes 'about a quarter of the eighth grade mathematics test score gap, more than a third of the advanced mathematics course enrollment gap, and a tenth of the eighth grade science test score gap' to 'the inequitable distribution of teachers.' The source's title is 'The role of teachers AND SCHOOLS in explaining STEM outcome gaps' - the decomposition is joint, and the teacher-specific share is smaller. These are also observational decompositions, not causal effects, but they appear under a heading asserting that inequitable access 'ha[s] negative consequences for students.' Go to Social Science Research 105, 102709 before quoting the figures.
- VERIFY BEFORE REPEATING - the '15% of SETs leave their schools annually (Gilmour et al., 2023)' figure. 'Leave their schools' should mean attrition plus moving, but this paper's own totals range from 16.8% (Pennsylvania) to 35.9% (Texas), and its attrition-only rates run 6.1% to 16.7%. Either the 15% is a national attrition rate mislabeled as school-leaving, or these seven states are far above the national school-leaving rate - and the paper never reconciles the two. Check Gilmour, Nguyen, Redding & Bettini (2023, RSE 44(3)) directly.
- VERIFY BEFORE REPEATING - 'SET turnover is consistently higher than turnover among other teachers (Billingsley & Bettini, 2019).' This paper's own Figure 3 refutes the universal version: SET attrition is NOT higher than general educator attrition in Massachusetts or Pennsylvania, and the gap is as small as 1.2 percentage points in Texas. Treat the SET-versus-general-education turnover gap as a context-dependent empirical question. This is arguably an underclaimed contribution of the paper - it is good evidence against a generalization the field repeats reflexively - but the paper states the generalization in the review and never revisits it.
- VERIFY BEFORE REPEATING - 'a recent study indicates that inequities in SET qualifications may have closed (Bettini, Nguyen, et al., 2022).' That study is national, survey-based (SASS/NTPS), and compares high- versus low-poverty schools; 'may have closed' is a strong gloss. The present paper's own results run the other way in several states (novices concentrated in high-FRPL schools in PA, VA, TX; lower certification in high-%Black and high-%Hispanic schools in MA, PA, VA). The tension is never addressed in the Discussion. Read both before citing either as settled.
- TREAT KALER ET AL. (2025) AS PRELIMINARY. It is an unpublished CALDER working paper (No. 319-0525) by authors overlapping this team, and the reference entry is corrupted (no publisher, no URL, because the duplicated Goldhaber & Theobald entry was interleaved into it). It supports the paper's causal-sounding claim that SET turnover lowers test scores for students with disabilities. Find the working paper at caldercenter.org and check its identification before relying on it.
- COMPANION READING - the causal state-policy evidence the review omits. For whether the differential-pay recommendation works: Theobald, Xu, Gilmour, Lachlan-Hache, Bettini & Jones (2025, EEPA) on the Hawaii \$10,000 SET bonus (cited here, and the single most relevant causal study); Feng & Sass on Florida's incentives for hard-to-staff subjects including special education; Clotfelter, Glennie, Ladd & Vigdor (2008) on the North Carolina bonus; Springer, Swain & Rodriguez (2016) on Tennessee. None but the first appears in this paper, which nonetheless recommends differential compensation in its Discussion.
- COMPANION READING - the sorting literature behind the paper's central mechanism. The finding that descriptive school-poverty turnover gaps vanish under controls because novice and uncertified SETs are sorted into those schools is the SET analogue of a well-established general-education result. Read Boyd, Lankford, Loeb & Wyckoff on teacher preferences and geographic proximity; Hanushek, Kain & Rivkin (2004); and Clotfelter, Ladd & Vigdor on teacher-quality gaps, to see how much of this pattern is SET-specific versus a labor-market regularity.
- COMPANION READING - before interpreting the charter results. The charter coefficients are among the largest in the paper (22.6-40.5 pp on novice status; 7.4-25.8 pp on attrition), and the paper offers only Weis, Woo & Nguyen (2024). Read alongside Stuit & Smith (2012) on charter teacher turnover, Torres (2016) on no-excuses schools, and the charter special-education enrollment literature (Winters; Setren). Crucially, check whether the states in question exempt charter teachers from certification requirements - that would mechanically produce the certification and novice gaps the paper reports as a workforce finding.
- COMPANION READING - FRPL measurement over exactly this period. Fazlul, Koedel & Parsons (2023) and Domina et al. (2018) document how the Community Eligibility Provision, and then USDA pandemic-era universal free meals in 2020-21 and 2021-22, degraded FRPL as a comparable poverty measure across states and over time. The paper's poverty-based equity results span 2017-18 to 2022-23 and rest entirely on within-state FRPL quartiles. Treat cross-state differences in the FRPL gradient (e.g., Pennsylvania's 10.1 pp high-versus-low-poverty turnover gap versus Texas's 1.4 pp) as partly a measurement artifact until shown otherwise.
- COMPANION READING - the counter-case on turnover harm. The review presents turnover as uniformly damaging. Read Adnot, Dee, Katz & Wyckoff (2017) on Washington DC, where turnover of low performers raised achievement, and Hanushek, Rivkin & Schiman (2016) on separating compositional from disruptive effects. Because this paper explicitly does not observe SET effectiveness (its own concluding limitation), its normative language - 'turnover of nearly half the workforce ... is clearly unsustainable' - is a policy judgment, not a finding.
- SITUATE THE SHORTAGE FRAMING CAREFULLY. The '45 states' and '49 states' shortage figures both trace to state self-designations under the federal Teacher Shortage Areas process, which triggers loan-forgiveness eligibility and is therefore over-declared. For a measure closer to actual unfilled positions, consult the national vacancy-tracking work (Nguyen, Lam & Bruno) rather than the designation counts. Do not read these numbers as shortage magnitudes.
- NOTE WHAT IS STRUCTURALLY ABSENT: the review builds no theory of state context. The paper's entire payoff is that SET challenges vary by state and therefore require state-specific policy - yet nothing in the literature review develops which state-level features (certification pathways and reciprocity, pension and salary schedules, caseload and class-size rules, special-education funding formulas, collective bargaining regimes, charter authorization law) should generate that variation. Readers should treat the cross-state differences as a well-measured set of facts awaiting explanation, not as evidence about which state policies matter.
- READ THE REFERENCE LIST WITH CARE IF YOU ARE CHASING SOURCES. Goldhaber & Theobald (2023) is duplicated with two different URLs; the Gershenson et al. (2022) DOI is broken ('https://0.1257/pol.20190573' - use https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20190573); Sorensen & Ladd is misspelled 'Sorenson' in the text; and there are two Digest of Education Statistics entries (NCES 2023 and U.S. Department of Education 2023) pointing at different tables, only one of which is cited. Also note that the sole authority for the linear-probability-model choice, von Hippel (2015), is a blog post.

**Detailed Commentary:**

OVERALL POSITION IN THE FIELD. This paper should be read as descriptive measurement infrastructure for a small subfield, not as a theory-testing or causal contribution, and its literature review is calibrated to that role - competently for the SET-specific literature, thinly for everything adjacent. The core diagnostic argument is correct and is the review's best moment: prior quantitative knowledge of the SET workforce comes either from nationally representative surveys that give cross-sectional snapshots (the SASS/NTPS lineage running through Mason-Williams 2015, Mason-Williams & Gagnon 2017, Bettini/Nguyen/Gilmour/Redding 2022, Bettini et al. 2025) or from single-state administrative studies (Theobald et al. 2021 in Washington), and the latter use incompatible definitions so that cross-state differences confound real variation with methodological choice. That is a genuine, correctly identified gap, and Gilmour, Feng & Theobald (2025) is the right citation for it. Everything good about the paper's positioning follows from that observation.

THE NOVELTY CLAIM, PRECISELY. The paper makes the claim four times, with drifting strength. The Introduction's version - 'the first cross-state study to longitudinally quantify the nature and magnitude of SET workforce challenges' - and the RQ section's 'first cross-state and with-in state analysis of the challenges facing the SET workforce' are the flat, oversold versions. The Discussion's 'first study to provide a comprehensive, longitudinal, cross-state evaluation of the composition, distribution, and stability' and the Conclusion's 'first to allow for comparisons ... by analyzing each state dataset in the same way' are the defensible versions, and the last one is exactly right. The reason the flat version fails is internal to the paper: the Stability section cites Pendola & Perrone (2025, AERA Open) for the claim that 'the rate at which SETs leave varies greatly across states,' which means cross-state longitudinal quantification of SET stability was already in print in a journal the authors read. The Discussion further concedes alignment with Pendola & Perrone on the paper's central regression finding. Beyond that, the broader multi-state teacher-labor-market literature - the CALDER supply-and-demand work the paper itself cites as Goldhaber, Falken & Theobald (2025), plus the general-education cross-state turnover base including Nguyen, Pham, Crouch & Springer's (2020) meta-analysis - means the methodological move of harmonizing multiple states is not new to education labor economics, only to special education. The right way for a reader to place this paper is: it is the first HARMONIZED cross-state SET study covering composition, distribution, and stability together. That is a real and useful claim, and it is the one the Conclusion actually makes.

A PARADOX WORTH NAMING. The paper oversells the substantive novelty and undersells the methodological one. The harmonization protocol is the contribution, but the two papers that document it - Gilmour, Feng & Theobald (2025, RSE) and Gilmour, Klinenberg, Bettini, Mason-Williams & Theobald (2026, TESE) - are relegated to two 'reported elsewhere' parentheticals. This is consequential for readers rather than merely stylistic, because the Discussion openly concedes that the two states with the lowest SET shares of the workforce (Indiana at 8.6%, Texas) are precisely the states where SETs were identified by classroom setting or student population served, which 'may have conflated SETs and general educators' and 'potentially inflated estimates of the rates of switching to general education in those states.' Texas has the highest total turnover in the paper (35.9%) and among the highest switching rates. So the single most striking cross-state comparison in the article - Texas 35.9% versus Pennsylvania 16.8% - has a live measurement explanation whose empirical treatment lives in a different journal. Any reader citing the Texas-Pennsylvania spread should read the TESE companion first.

WHOSE LITERATURE IS THIS. Roughly half of the fifty-odd references involve at least one of the nine coauthors. Bettini appears in four entries, Gilmour in four, Mason-Williams in four, Theobald in six or seven counting the Goldhaber collaborations, and Scott, Redding, Feng, and Nguyen in others. I want to be careful here: SET workforce research is a genuinely small field, and Billingsley, Bettini, Mason-Williams, Sindelar, McLeskey, Gilmour, and Theobald substantially constitute it. Citing them is not self-dealing; it is citing the field. But the practical consequence for a reader is that the 'state of knowledge' this review reports is largely a single research group's prior findings, and where those findings are contested or preliminary the review does not surface the contest. The clearest case is the framing claim that SET turnover is consistently higher than general educator turnover, sourced to Billingsley & Bettini (2019) - a claim this paper's own Figure 3 refutes in two of seven states.

ENGAGEMENT WITH CONFLICTING EVIDENCE - MIXED, WITH ONE GENUINE STRENGTH AND THREE UNADDRESSED TENSIONS. The strength: the paper states plainly that its special-education-school results contrast with Mason-Williams & Gagnon (2017) and Mason-Williams, Bettini & Gagnon (2017), both SASS-based, and it does so in the Discussion where it counts, noting the certification exception. Since Mason-Williams is a coauthor, contradicting her own prior work in print is a real credibility signal. The unaddressed tensions: (1) The review cites Bettini, Nguyen et al. (2022) for the proposition that 'inequities in SET qualifications may have closed,' then produces findings across several states showing novices concentrated in high-FRPL schools and lower certification in schools with higher shares of Black and Hispanic students - and never returns to the contradiction. (2) It asserts SET turnover exceeds general-education turnover, then shows it does not in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania and by only 1.2 points in Texas, and the Discussion never revisits the generalization. (3) It presents turnover as uniformly harmful, citing Ronfeldt et al. (2013), Sorensen & Ladd (2020), Kaler et al. (2025), and Synar & Maiden (2012) - all one direction - while omitting the compositional counter-case (Adnot, Dee, Katz & Wyckoff 2017; Hanushek, Rivkin & Schiman 2016). The third omission matters most because the paper's own final limitation concedes it observes no student outcomes and no SET effectiveness, which makes 'turnover of nearly half the workforce ... is clearly unsustainable' a policy stance rather than a finding.

ADJACENT LITERATURES A READER SHOULD SUPPLY. Four gaps change how the results read. First, compensation. The Discussion recommends 'differential compensation program[s], such as Hawaii's' on the strength of one citation. The causal literature on subject-targeted incentives - Clotfelter, Glennie, Ladd & Vigdor (2008); Springer, Swain & Rodriguez (2016); and especially Feng & Sass on Florida's incentives for hard-to-staff subjects including special education - is absent even though Li Feng is a coauthor. Second, sorting. The paper's headline mechanism (descriptive school-poverty turnover gaps are driven by the distribution of novice and uncertified SETs, not by differential treatment within schools) recapitulates a general-education finding with a long pedigree - Boyd/Lankford/Loeb/Wyckoff on preferences and proximity, Hanushek/Kain/Rivkin (2004), Clotfelter/Ladd/Vigdor on teacher-quality gaps - none of which appear in the Discussion where the mechanism is asserted. Third, charters. The charter coefficients are the largest in the paper (a 22.6-40.5 percentage point increase in the probability a SET is a novice; 7.4-25.8 points on attrition), supported by one citation, and the review never mentions that many states exempt charter teachers from certification requirements. That exemption is a mechanical explanation for the certification and novice gaps, and a reader who does not supply it will mis-attribute the pattern to working conditions. Fourth, poverty measurement. The entire FRPL-based equity analysis spans 2017-18 to 2022-23, a window that includes both accelerating Community Eligibility Provision adoption and USDA universal free meals in 2020-21 and 2021-22. Fazlul, Koedel & Parsons (2023) and Domina et al. (2018) document how badly this degrades FRPL comparability. The paper shows local awareness (substituting Massachusetts DESE economic-disadvantage data) without ever engaging the general problem. Cross-state comparisons of the FRPL gradient should carry that caveat.

TWO SMALLER MISCITATIONS. Chingos & Peterson (2011) and Nguyen, Pham, Crouch & Springer (2020) are cited jointly for 'higher attrition rates, AND rapid growth in effectiveness, in the first 3 years.' Nguyen et al. (2020) is a turnover meta-analysis; it supports the attrition half, not the returns-to-experience half. The standard citations for early-career effectiveness growth (Papay & Kraft 2015; Wiswall 2013; Rice) do not appear. Separately, von Hippel (2015) - a Statistical Horizons blog post - is the sole authority for the choice of linear probability models over logistic regression, where Angrist & Pischke or Wooldridge would be the peer-reviewed citations. Neither error is fatal; both are the kind of thing a reader chasing a claim should know before following the footnote.

REFERENCE-LIST HYGIENE. Four concrete defects. (a) Goldhaber & Theobald (2023, CALDER Policy Brief 32-0223) appears twice with two different URLs, and the duplicate is interleaved directly after the Kaler et al. (2025) entry - which is why Kaler et al. is left with a bare '(Working Paper No. 319-0525)' and no publisher, institution, or link. That is the one unpublished source carrying a causal claim about turnover harming students with disabilities, so the missing provenance is unfortunate. (b) The Gershenson, Hart, Hyman, Lindsay & Papageorge (2022) DOI is malformed as 'https://0.1257/pol.20190573'; the correct form is https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20190573. (c) Sorensen & Ladd (2020) is cited in text as 'Sorenson & Ladd.' (d) Two Digest of Education Statistics entries exist - National Center for Education Statistics (2023) pointing at table dt23_203.70 and U.S. Department of Education (2023) pointing at dt23_204.70 - and only the latter appears to be cited in text. Alphabetization also breaks in the Gilmour and Goldhaber runs. None of this affects the findings; all of it costs a reader time.

WHAT IS STRUCTURALLY MISSING. The deepest limitation of the positioning is not any particular absent citation but the absence of a theory of state context. The paper's entire argument is that SET workforce challenges vary by state and therefore demand state-specific policy responses. Yet the literature review never develops which features of state context - certification pathways and license reciprocity, salary schedules and pension structures, caseload and class-size regulation, special-education funding formulas, collective bargaining regimes, charter authorization law - should be expected to produce that variation. The Discussion gestures at several of these post hoc ('States also have different preparation and certification requirements, compensation and retirement packages, and working conditions'), but they are not set up in advance and generate no testable expectations. The consequence for readers is that the paper delivers a well-measured set of cross-state facts awaiting explanation. Cite it for the facts. Do not cite it for what makes states differ.

CONFIDENCE. I rate this adequate rather than weak because the review covers the core SET workforce literature correctly, maps cleanly onto the research questions, and is honest about at least one contradiction with prior work including a coauthor's own. I rate it adequate rather than strong because of the oversold flat novelty claim, the heavy self-referentiality, four substantively consequential adjacent-literature gaps, at least three prior findings stated more flatly than they hold, and real reference-list errors.
