My confidence is moderate (0.72): I know the general-education teacher labor market and sorting literatures well and the SET workforce literature reasonably, but I could not access the supplementary materials or the OSF repository, could not open the cited sources to confirm the specific figures I flagged for verification, and cannot rule out that some work I list as missing is discussed in the online supplement. The verification flags above are stated as things a reader should check, not as confirmed misstatements.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is cleanly organized, plainly written, and admirably disciplined about hedging its descriptive design in most places; the prose moves a seven-state, six-table analysis along without bogging down, and the large majority of specific point estimates quoted in the text match the tables exactly. But the article has an unusually high density of text-vs-table disagreements that survived production, concentrated in exactly the kind of sentence readers are most likely to quote: the universal-quantifier summaries ('in all states except X,' 'across all states,' 'only in Texas'). At least three of these are outright wrong (a sign reversal, a wrong exception state, and a claim contradicted for four states), the Figure 3 panel labels are swapped between caption and text, and the Discussion/Conclusion repeatedly drop hedges the Results had carefully attached.

**Strengths:**

- Structure is genuinely easy to navigate: three research questions (composition, distribution, stability) map one-to-one onto three Results subsections, each split into descriptive-then-regression, and each further split by school level/type/urbanicity vs. school/district student characteristics. A reader can jump directly to the subsection they need.
- Variables section is exemplary and load-bearing. Each construct gets its own labeled subsection stating the coding, the reference category for regressions, the CEDS alignment, and the state-specific exceptions (no degree data in HI and IN; 18.8% missing race in VA; DESE economic-disadvantage substitute in MA). Readers evaluating cross-state comparability have everything they need in one place.
- The 'Deviations from Preregistration' section is unusually candid and specific, naming three categories of departure (sample, variables, analytic plan) with reasons. This is rare and directly useful to readers assessing how much the analysis was shaped after the fact.
- Most quantitative claims are exactly right. Spot-checking every number in the Results against Tables 1-6: the middle-school novice figures (TX 1.4 / MA 1.5 / HI 5.5; PA 1.6 / VA 2.6 / WA 2.6), the special-education-school certification range (6.7 to 73.5 pp), the certification-switching range (3.7 to 40.3 pp), the novice attrition contrast (PA 1.9 vs. HI 10.1), the certification-attrition contrast (TX -18.8 vs. VA -2.4), the charter novice range (22.6-40.5 pp), and the special-education-school attrition figures (MA 6.1 / TX 4.9 / WA 4.1; VA +21.4) all reproduce the table cells to the decimal.
- The Limitations section is substantive rather than perfunctory: five distinct limitations, each tied to a concrete analytic consequence (experience miscoding, excluded nondistrict SETs, coarse ethnoracial categories, missing general-educator benchmarks for most analyses, no student outcomes).
- The framing of ethnoracial aggregation ('findings based on this aggregation should be interpreted as revealing insights into the operations of racism in education, not the characteristics of the people aggregated') is stated once in Methods and honored again in Limitations. Consistent and clear.
- The Discussion's opening enumeration of four noteworthy findings gives a time-constrained reader a defensible one-paragraph takeaway.

**Weaknesses:**

- SIGN REVERSAL. 'SETs of color moved schools at a higher rate than White teachers only in Texas (Table 6).' Table 6's SET-of-color row is HI -0.0079, IN -0.0052, MA -0.0037, PA 0.0066, TX -0.0040*, VA 0.0016, WA 0.0058. Texas is the only significant cell and it is NEGATIVE: SETs of color in Texas moved at a LOWER rate. The direction in the text is backwards.
- WRONG EXCEPTION STATE (1). 'In all states except Washington, stability for SETs of color varied from that for White SETs.' Massachusetts is equally an exception: MA's SET-of-color coefficient is nonsignificant in all three stability tables (Table 4: 0.0119, SE 0.0083; Table 5: 0.0094, SE 0.0089; Table 6: -0.0037, SE 0.0063). MA and WA are statistically indistinguishable here, yet only WA is named.
- WRONG EXCEPTION STATE (2). 'In all states except HawaiI, school level was associated with stability' (note also the capitalization typo). Hawaii in fact has significant school-level coefficients in every one of Tables 4-6 (Table 4 middle school 0.0295**, Table 5 middle 0.0177* and high 0.0220*, Table 6 high school -0.0182*). The state with NO significant school-level coefficient anywhere in Tables 4-6 is Indiana. The exception appears to have been swapped.
- CLAIM CONTRADICTED IN FOUR STATES. 'Across most states, a lower percentage of high school SETs switched to general education or moved compared with elementary SETs.' True for moving (six of seven negative and significant in Table 6), but false for switching: Table 5's high-school row is significantly POSITIVE in Hawaii (0.0220*), Massachusetts (0.0473***), Texas (0.0335***), and Virginia (0.0205***), and negative in only PA and WA. The 'or' construction lets a reader carry the moving result over onto switching.
- DISCUSSION CONTRADICTS ITS OWN RESULTS. Discussion: 'In Pennsylvania and Indiana, SETs of color were (a) more likely to work in schools serving higher percentages of students eligible for FRPL or students of color.' Table 2's school % FRPL cell for Pennsylvania is -0.0048* (and district % FRPL -0.0087***) - significantly NEGATIVE - and Indiana's is 0.0040 (SE 0.0058), null. The Results section says the opposite in plain terms ('In Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, SETs in schools and districts with higher percentages of students eligible for FRPL were less likely to be SETs of color'). Only the 'students of color' half of the disjunction holds (PA school % Black 0.0607***, IN 0.0650***).
- OVERSTATED UNIVERSALS. 'Across all states, SETs in schools with higher enrollments were less likely to move schools (Table 6)' - Hawaii's cell is -0.0023 with SE 0.0024, nonsignificant (six of seven, not all). 'In most states, novices had higher probabilities of attrition' is followed by a PA-to-HI range that silently omits Texas, whose novice attrition coefficient is -0.0015 (ns) - the one state where novices are not at higher risk. 'Across states with charter school options, SETs had higher attrition ... with differences from 7.4 to 25.8 percentage points' omits Virginia's 0.0034 (ns), which is not in the stated range.
- DE-HEDGING BETWEEN RESULTS AND DISCUSSION. The Results carefully say 'Within most states, SETs in charter schools were ... less likely to be fully certified'; the Discussion drops the qualifier: 'in states with a charter sector, charter schools were staffed by higher percentages of novice SETs and lower percentages of fully certified SETs.' Virginia contradicts both halves (Table 3 charter +0.0930*, significantly MORE certified; Table 1 charter 0.0915, ns). Same pattern for 'Even after accounting for teacher characteristics, across states, higher percentages of SETs in charter schools left teaching' (VA 0.0034, ns), and for 'in some states (i.e., Texas and Washington), SETs in special education schools had lower predicted probabilities of all types of turnover' (WA's moving coefficient is 0.0015, ns and positive).
- RHETORIC OUTRUNNING THE NUMBER. Discussion: 'turnover of nearly half the workforce (which we found in one state and in some locations in other states) is clearly unsustainable.' The highest state total turnover the paper reports is Texas at 35.9%. Nothing in the article supports a statewide rate near 50%.
- CAUSAL ESCALATION IN THE CONCLUSION. The Discussion hedges properly ('may underlie,' 'it appeared that ... may be due to'); the Conclusion, where many readers stop, states flatly that 'higher turnover in schools serving more marginalized student populations was likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs across settings.' No mediation analysis is presented anywhere - the support is that descriptive gaps attenuate once teacher characteristics enter the LPMs, which is consistent with but does not establish that mechanism.
- FIGURE 3 PANELS SWAPPED. The caption reads 'Attrition (top) and full certification (bottom).' The text says 'The top panel of Figure 3 shows the percentage of SETs in each state who were fully certified' and, later, 'The bottom panel of Figure 3 illustrates the proportion of SETs ... who left teaching in their state each year.' Caption and text disagree, consistently and in both directions; a reader cannot tell which is right without opening the figure.
- FIGURE 5 CAPTION MISDESCRIBES THE FIGURE. Caption: 'Attrition distribution by school free or reduced-price lunch quartile (top) and school students of color quartile (bottom).' Text: 'Figure 5 illustrates three types of turnover: attrition ... switching ... and moving,' and every number the text pulls from it is TOTAL turnover (PA 16.8%, TX 35.9%, the 10.1 pp and 9.3 pp and 7.2 pp quartile gaps), not attrition. Anyone citing Figure 5 from the caption alone will cite the wrong quantity.
- MOST DESCRIPTIVE NUMBERS ARE UNVERIFIABLE FROM THE ARTICLE. Every level and trend the paper quotes - 8.6% to 18.4% SETs of the workforce, 19.8-33.6% novices, 28.8% to 67.3% advanced degrees, PA 6.1% vs. VA 16.7% attrition, PA 16.8% vs. TX 35.9% total turnover, the 5.6-9.6 pp certification gaps, the 1.2-5.5 pp SET-vs-general-educator attrition gaps - lives only in Figures 1-5. The tables carry only regression coefficients. There is no descriptive-statistics table in the article.
- TWO COMPOSITION OUTCOMES HAVE NO TABLE. The text makes repeated claims about advanced degrees ('more likely to have advanced degrees in middle and high schools ... consistent across states except in Texas'; charter SETs 'less likely to have advanced degrees') and about gender, but only novice status, SET-of-color status, and full certification get tables. Those regressions are OSF-only, and OSF is the only place full regression results live for anything.
- TABLE NOTES ARE NOT SELF-CONTAINED. Nothing in any table note explains the blank cells - Hawaii has no charter or district rows (it is a single-district state, mentioned only late in the Discussion), pre-K appears in three columns, CTE in three. Table 2's Virginia N (87,217) is ~21,000 smaller than Tables 1 and 3 (108,623) with no explanation, even though Methods says the VA missing-race cases were handled with an indicator rather than dropped. Ns also vary across Tables 4, 5, and 6 for the same state and same analytic sample (Indiana: 12,507 / 13,822 / 12,892 - switching has MORE observations than attrition), unexplained.
- A STAR THAT DOES NOT MATCH ITS STANDARD ERROR. Table 4, District % English learner, Pennsylvania: 0.0067* with SE 0.0044 (t = 1.52). The Results sentence 'In Pennsylvania ... SETs in districts with more English learners were more likely to leave teaching in the state' rests on this cell.
- COPYEDITING ERRORS THAT SURVIVED PRODUCTION: an unfinished sentence - 'associated with a in the 0.5-1.5 percentage point change in the stability outcome'; 'FRRL' for FRPL in the Figure 5 discussion; 'with-in state' in the Research Questions; 'HawaiI'; 'Sorenson & Ladd, 2020' in text vs. 'Sorensen, L. C., & Ladd, H. F.' in the reference list; a Goldhaber & Theobald (2023) entry duplicated in the reference list (the duplicate is spliced in right after the Kaler et al. entry, which itself has no publisher); and a malformed DOI for Gershenson et al. ('https://0.1257/...').
- SUPPLEMENT CROSS-REFERENCE ERROR. The Discussion sends readers to 'Supplementary Appendix Table 3A' for the FRPL quartile cutoffs, but Methods says quartile information is in Table 4A and that Table 3A holds the certification-area crosswalk. The supplement numbering is also inconsistently formatted (Table A1 vs. Tables 3A/4A/5A/6A/7A, Figures 1A/2A).
- AMBIGUOUS SENTENCE WITH A WRONG CITATION. 'The association between SETs in charter schools and switching to general education or moving schools was not statistically significant in all states (Table 6).' 'Not significant in all states' can be read as 'significant in none' - which is false (Table 5 PA 0.0564*** and TX 0.0563***; Table 6 TX 0.0966*** and WA 0.101*) - and the sentence covers switching but cites only Table 6.
- THE ABSTRACT IS ACCURATE BUT NEARLY CONTENT-FREE. It contains no numbers, does not name the seven states, does not give the years, does not say the data are state longitudinal administrative records, and does not state that the design is descriptive/associational. It does avoid causal language, and 'These findings suggest' is properly hedged - so it will not mislead, but a reader who stops at the abstract learns essentially nothing they could cite.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the Method's 'Variables' subsections before anything else. The cross-state comparability of every result in the paper is determined there - especially the note that inexperience was constructed from the first three years of data rather than from reported experience, and that SETs were identified by fundamentally different mechanisms across states (an indicator in HI, assignment codes in MA/PA/VA, student population served in TX, classroom setting in IN, funding source in WA).
- Do not quote any 'in all states,' 'across all states,' 'in each state,' or 'only in [state]' sentence without checking the row yourself. This is where the paper's errors cluster. Specifically verify before citing: the SET-of-color moving direction in Texas (Table 6 is NEGATIVE, not positive, contrary to the text); the 'all states except Washington' claim about SETs of color (Massachusetts is equally null across Tables 4-6); the 'all states except Hawaii' school-level claim (Hawaii is significant in all three tables; Indiana is the state with nothing significant); and 'across all states, SETs in schools with higher enrollments were less likely to move schools' (Hawaii is nonsignificant).
- Treat the Discussion's Pennsylvania/Indiana sentence about SETs of color and FRPL as unreliable. Table 2 shows PA's school and district FRPL coefficients for SETs of color are significantly NEGATIVE, and IN's are null. The Results section says so explicitly. Only the 'higher percentages of students of color' half of that Discussion claim is supported.
- For descriptive rates - attrition, total turnover, percent novice, percent SETs of color, certification gaps - go to Figures 1-5, not the tables. There is no descriptive-statistics table in the article. If you need a specific state-year rate rather than the article's rounded summary, the authors' data explorer (sparccenter.org) and the OSF repository are the only sources.
- Tables 1-3 (composition/distribution LPMs) and Tables 4-6 (attrition/switching/moving LPMs) are the load-bearing exhibits, and they are self-contained enough to read cold. If you have time for only two things, read Table 4 (attrition) and Table 3 (full certification) - the certification result is the paper's strongest and most consistent finding (negative and significant in all seven states in Table 4; special education schools significantly less certified in all seven in Table 3).
- Read Figure 3 with the panel labels in question. The caption says attrition is the top panel; the text says certification is the top panel. Determine which from the axis labels before citing 'the top panel of Figure 3.'
- Read Figure 5's caption as a mislabel. The caption says 'attrition distribution,' but every number the text draws from Figure 5 is TOTAL turnover (attrition + switching + moving) by quartile. Cite it as total turnover, and note that the caption's 'Middle' means the middle two quartiles pooled.
- You can skim the literature review (pp. 2-4) and the Deviations from Preregistration section on a first pass, but do not skip the Limitations - the first limitation (variables that look comparable across states are not comparable in practice) is the single most important caveat for anyone doing cross-state comparisons with these numbers, and it is stated only there.
- Stop at the Discussion; treat the Conclusion's 'likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs' as an overstatement. The Discussion's own phrasing ('may be due to,' 'it appeared that') is the defensible version. No mediation or decomposition is presented.
- Do not repeat the Discussion's 'turnover of nearly half the workforce ... in one state.' The highest state figure the article reports is 35.9% (Texas).
- Anything about advanced degrees or gender in the composition analyses is asserted without a table in the article - the regressions are on OSF only. Check the OSF repository before quoting those.
- When comparing Ns across tables, expect unexplained variation: Table 2's Virginia N is ~21,000 smaller than Tables 1 and 3 (almost certainly the 18.8% with missing race/ethnicity, though Methods implies an indicator was used instead of dropping them), and Tables 4-6 differ from each other within state. If sample composition matters to your use of the paper, resolve this against the OSF materials rather than assuming a common sample.
- One table cell to distrust: Table 4, District % English learner, Pennsylvania (0.0067 with SE 0.0044) is starred at p < .05 but implies t = 1.52. The Results sentence about Pennsylvania districts with more English learners and attrition depends on it.
- Indiana's coefficients should be read with the paper's own caveat in hand. Its switching coefficients are enormous (fully certified -0.403 in Table 5, a 40.3 pp difference), and the Discussion itself notes that identifying SETs by classroom setting (IN) or student population served (TX) 'may have conflated SETs and general educators ... and potentially inflated estimates of the rates of switching to general education in those states.' That caveat appears only in the Discussion, well after the Results present the number without qualification. Indiana also covers only 2017-18 to 2019-20, i.e., almost none of the post-COVID period the paper elsewhere emphasizes.

**Detailed Commentary:**

ORGANIZATION AND NAVIGABILITY. The paper is well-built and, for a seven-state, three-question, six-table article, remarkably easy to move through. Three research questions map cleanly onto three Results subsections; each begins with descriptive results and then turns to regression results; each regression subsection is further partitioned into 'School Level, Type, and Urbanicity' and 'School and District Student Characteristics,' with the same headings reused in the Stability section so a reader learns the pattern once. The Method's Variables section is the paper's best-written stretch: every construct is defined, its coding stated, its reference category for regressions named, its CEDS alignment noted, and its state-specific exceptions listed inline. That is where the load-bearing material for interpreting anything else lives, and it is easy to find. The Discussion opens with four numbered takeaways, which gives a hurried reader something defensible to carry away.

The navigability failure is at the level of what is IN the article versus what is on OSF. The article prints only coefficient tables (Tables 1-6). There is no descriptive-statistics table anywhere. Every level, rate, and trend the prose quotes - 8.6% to 18.4% of the workforce being SETs, 19.8-33.6% novices, 28.8% (TX) to 67.3% (WA) with advanced degrees, 88.0-94.9% White in four states, 66.6% SETs of color in Hawaii, PA attrition 6.1% vs. VA 16.7%, PA total turnover 16.8% vs. TX 35.9%, the 5.6-9.6 pp SET-vs-general-educator certification gaps, the 1.2 pp (TX) to 5.5 pp (VA) attrition gaps, the 10.1 pp / 1.4 pp / 9.3 pp / 2.2 pp / 7.2 pp quartile turnover gaps - is readable only off Figures 1-5, which are graphs, not tables. A reader who wants a number rather than the article's rounded prose version cannot get it from the article. Two of the five composition outcomes (advanced degree, gender) get no table at all despite being discussed in the text, and 'full regression results' for everything are OSF-only.

FIDELITY: WHAT CHECKS OUT. I verified every numeric claim in the Results and Discussion against Tables 1-6, reconstructing column alignment (HI, IN, MA, PA, TX, VA, WA) from value counts. The great majority reproduce exactly. Middle-school novice: text says TX 1.4, MA 1.5, HI 5.5 pp more likely; Table 1 gives 0.0139***, 0.0145*, 0.0553**. Text says PA 1.6, VA 2.6, WA 2.6 less likely; Table 1 gives -0.0160***, -0.0258***, -0.0264**. 'Not significant in Hawaii or Massachusetts' for high school novice: Table 1 HI -0.0389 (SE 0.0283), MA -0.0005 (SE 0.0084), both null - correct. Hawaii city -5.8 pp and Washington city +2.1 pp: -0.0578** and 0.0208*, correct. Charter novice 22.6-40.5 pp: TX 0.226*** and WA 0.405***, correct. Special-education-school certification 6.7 to 73.5 pp: TX -0.0673** and HI -0.735***, correct. Novice attrition PA 1.9 vs. HI 10.1: 0.0193*** and 0.101***, correct. Switching novice range 1.6-4.5: WA 0.0158*** and IN 0.0453***, correct. Moving novice range 1.2-6.9: HI 0.0120* and WA 0.0694***, correct. Certification-attrition TX -18.8 vs. VA -2.4: -0.1880*** and -0.0240***, correct, and 'in each state' is right - all seven cells in Table 4's certification row are negative and significant. Certification-switching 3.7 to 40.3 pp and 'all states except Virginia': HI -0.0372**, IN -0.403***, VA 0.0023 (ns), correct. 'Except in Hawaii, fully certified SETs were more likely to move': Table 6 HI -0.0262*, all six others positive and significant, correct. Special-education-school attrition 4.1-6.1 pp in MA/TX/WA and +21.4 in VA: -0.0607*, -0.0489***, -0.0409**, +0.214***, correct. 'Less likely to switch ... in all states' and 'in four states also less likely to move': Table 5 all seven negative, Table 6 four negative and significant (HI, IN, PA, TX), correct. 'Attrition ... not associated with school % FRPL in any state': all seven Table 4 cells unstarred, correct. 'Within four states, switching or moving increased as low-income proportion increased': union of Table 5 (HI, MA, PA) and Table 6 (PA, TX) is exactly four states, correct. The Texas district-%-Black and district-%-EL claims all check out. This is a paper whose author-level arithmetic is careful; the failures are in the quantifiers, not the numbers.

FIDELITY: WHAT DOES NOT. Five text-vs-table problems are serious enough that a reader must not quote the sentence.

(1) Sign reversal. 'SETs of color moved schools at a higher rate than White teachers only in Texas (Table 6).' Table 6's SET-of-color row reads HI -0.0079 (0.0054), IN -0.0052 (0.0139), MA -0.0037 (0.0063), PA 0.0066 (0.0049), TX -0.0040* (0.0019), VA 0.0016 (0.0027), WA 0.0058 (0.0063). Texas is indeed the only significant cell, but it is negative: Texas SETs of color moved at a LOWER rate. The text has the direction backwards.

(2) Wrong exception state, SETs of color. 'In all states except Washington, stability for SETs of color varied from that for White SETs.' Washington is null in all three tables (Table 4 -0.0002, Table 5 0.0017, Table 6 0.0058) - and so is Massachusetts (Table 4 0.0119 with SE 0.0083; Table 5 0.0094 with SE 0.0089; Table 6 -0.0037 with SE 0.0063). The sentence should read 'except Washington and Massachusetts.' Note also that Virginia's Table 4 attrition coefficient is literally 0.0000; VA survives the claim only via Table 5's switching coefficient (-0.0143***).

(3) Wrong exception state, school level. 'In all states except HawaiI, school level was associated with stability, but the direction and magnitude of associations varied (Tables 4-6).' Hawaii has significant school-level coefficients in all three: Table 4 middle school 0.0295** (SE 0.0110), Table 5 middle 0.0177* and high 0.0220*, Table 6 high school -0.0182*. The state with no significant school-level coefficient anywhere in Tables 4-6 is INDIANA (middle/high/other all null in each). This reads like a substituted state name.

(4) Half-true 'or' claim. 'Across most states, a lower percentage of high school SETs switched to general education or moved compared with elementary SETs.' The moving half is right (Table 6 high-school row is negative and significant in six of seven). The switching half is wrong in four states: Table 5's high-school row is 0.0220* (HI), 0.0473*** (MA), 0.0335*** (TX), 0.0205*** (VA) - significantly MORE switching - and negative only in PA (-0.0080***) and WA (-0.0304***). Read literally, 'across most states' applies to a disjunction, but any reader will take away 'high school SETs switch less,' which is the opposite of what four states show.

(5) A Discussion sentence contradicted by the paper's own Results. Discussion: 'In Pennsylvania and Indiana, SETs of color were (a) more likely to work in schools serving higher percentages of students eligible for FRPL or students of color and (b) more likely to leave teaching in the state.' Part (b) is right (Table 4: IN 0.0334*, PA 0.0319***). Part (a) is wrong on the FRPL half: Table 2's school % FRPL is -0.0048* for Pennsylvania (and district % FRPL -0.0087***), significantly negative, and 0.0040 (SE 0.0058) for Indiana, null. The Results section had said this plainly and correctly: 'In Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, SETs in schools and districts with higher percentages of students eligible for FRPL were less likely to be SETs of color.' Only the 'students of color' half of the Discussion's disjunction holds (school % Black: PA 0.0607***, IN 0.0650***). A reader quoting the Discussion will state the opposite of what Table 2 shows for Pennsylvania.

A further tier of overstatements is milder but systematic: universals stated where six of seven states qualify. 'Across all states, SETs in schools with higher enrollments were less likely to move schools (Table 6)' - Hawaii is -0.0023 with SE 0.0024, t < 1. 'In most states, novices had higher probabilities of attrition, switching, and moving,' followed by a PA-to-HI range, quietly omits Texas, whose novice attrition coefficient is -0.0015 (ns) - the substantively interesting exception. 'Across states with charter school options, SETs had higher attrition ... with differences from 7.4 to 25.8 percentage points' omits Virginia (0.0034, ns), which falls outside the stated range. The stated ranges are consistently ranges over the SIGNIFICANT cells only, without saying so, so a reader who assumes the range spans all seven states will be wrong every time.

DE-HEDGING FROM RESULTS TO DISCUSSION TO CONCLUSION. There is a visible gradient. The Results say 'Within most states, SETs in charter schools were less experienced ... and less likely to be fully certified'; the Discussion says, unqualified, 'in states with a charter sector, charter schools were staffed by higher percentages of novice SETs and lower percentages of fully certified SETs than traditional public schools.' Virginia contradicts both halves - Table 3's charter cell for VA is +0.0930*, significantly MORE certified, and Table 1's is 0.0915 (ns). Same for 'across states, higher percentages of SETs in charter schools left teaching' (VA 0.0034, ns), and for 'in some states (i.e., Texas and Washington), SETs in special education schools had lower predicted probabilities of all types of turnover' - Washington's Table 6 moving coefficient is 0.0015 (ns, and positive), so 'all types' fails. The Discussion also asserts 'turnover of nearly half the workforce (which we found in one state and in some locations in other states),' when the highest statewide total turnover reported anywhere is Texas at 35.9%. And the Conclusion escalates the paper's carefully associational language into a mechanism: 'higher turnover in schools serving more marginalized student populations was likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs across settings.' The Discussion's own version - 'it appeared that descriptive within-state differences in stability across schools and districts may be due to the unequal distribution of SET characteristics' - is the supportable one. Nothing in the paper is a mediation analysis; the evidence is that descriptive gaps shrink when teacher characteristics are added, which the authors report honestly ('associations declined in magnitude by nearly half after the addition of school characteristics' in IN and PA) but which does not license 'driven by.' Readers should note this is the paper's last substantive sentence before the policy call, i.e., the one most likely to be quoted.

One more claim readers cannot check and should treat carefully: the Supplemental Analyses paragraph states that discrete-time hazard models show 'in many states, SETs of color or novice SETs had higher probabilities of attrition than White SETs or SETs with prior experience.' The main Table 4 shows SETs of color with SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER attrition in Hawaii (-0.0865***) and Texas (-0.0213***) and higher in only two states (IN, PA). The 'X or Y' construction fuses a robust novice finding with a heterogeneous SET-of-color finding into a single sentence that reads as if both hold in many states. The hazard models cover only early-career SETs and live on OSF, so this cannot be adjudicated from the article - which is precisely why the sentence should not be quoted.

EXHIBITS AND CROSS-REFERENCES. Figure 3 is the worst offender. Its caption reads 'Attrition (top) and full certification (bottom)'; the text says twice, in different sections, the reverse - 'The top panel of Figure 3 shows the percentage of SETs in each state who were fully certified' and 'The bottom panel of Figure 3 illustrates the proportion of SETs and the proportion of general educators ... who left teaching.' Figure 5's caption calls it 'Attrition distribution by school free or reduced-price lunch quartile (top) and school students of color quartile (bottom),' but the text describes it as showing three turnover types and every figure the text extracts from it (16.8%, 35.9%, 10.1 pp, 1.4 pp, 9.3 pp, 2.2 pp, 7.2 pp) is TOTAL turnover. The same sentence contains 'FRRL' for FRPL. The Discussion sends readers to 'Supplementary Appendix Table 3A' for FRPL quartile cutoffs, but Methods assigns quartile information to Table 4A and certification areas to Table 3A. Supplement numbering itself alternates conventions (Table A1 in one place, Tables 3A/4A/5A/6A/7A and Figures 1A/2A elsewhere). And 'The association between SETs in charter schools and switching to general education or moving schools was not statistically significant in all states (Table 6)' is both ambiguously worded (it means 'not significant in every state,' which is true - PA and TX are significant for switching, TX and WA for moving) and cites only Table 6 for a sentence that covers Table 5.

The tables themselves are readable but not self-contained. Nothing explains Hawaii's blank district and charter rows (single-district state - mentioned only deep in the Discussion), or why pre-K appears in three columns and CTE in three. Table 2's Virginia N is 87,217 against 108,623 in Tables 1 and 3, consistent with dropping the 18.8% missing race cases, but Methods says an indicator was used - the discrepancy is never addressed. Tables 4, 5, and 6 report different Ns for the same state (Indiana 12,507 / 13,822 / 12,892; Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361), with switching sometimes estimated on MORE observations than attrition, and no note explains it. Finally, one cell's significance marker does not match its standard error: Table 4, District % English learner, Pennsylvania is 0.0067* with SE 0.0044 (t = 1.52), and the Results sentence about Pennsylvania districts with more English learners and attrition depends on that star.

ABSTRACT FIDELITY. The abstract is accurate and non-overclaiming - there is no causal language, and 'These findings suggest a need for policies and practices that vary by state context' is the right strength. It also conveys the paper's genuine organizing insight (some challenges similar across states, others varying by and within state). What it does not do is inform. It contains no numbers, does not name the seven states, does not give the years (2017-18 to 2022-23), does not say the data are state longitudinal administrative records covering hundreds of thousands of teacher-years, and does not state that the design is descriptive and associational rather than causal. A reader who stops at the abstract will not be misled, but will also have nothing citable. Given that the study's headline value is precisely the cross-state magnitudes, the absence of even one range (e.g., total turnover 16.8% to 35.9%) is a missed opportunity rather than a fidelity failure.

PROSE-LEVEL LAPSES THAT SURVIVED PRODUCTION. An unfinished sentence at the end of the Stability results: 'associations between a 1 standard deviation change in the school or district student characteristics associated with a in the 0.5-1.5 percentage point change in the stability outcome.' 'with-in state' in the Research Questions. 'HawaiI.' 'FRRL.' 'Sorenson & Ladd, 2020' in text against 'Sorensen, L. C., & Ladd, H. F.' in the reference list. A duplicated Goldhaber & Theobald (2023) entry spliced into the reference list immediately after Kaler et al. (2025), which itself lacks a publisher. A malformed DOI for Gershenson et al. ('https://0.1257/pol.20190573'). The stability variables are called 'four mutually exclusive turnover categories' when one of the four is staying. Individually trivial; collectively they suggest the copyediting pass that would have caught the Figure 3 panel mismatch and the sign reversal did not happen.

BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS. This is a clear, well-structured, genuinely useful descriptive paper whose numbers are mostly right and whose framing is mostly honest. But its summary sentences - the ones that generalize across states, which are exactly the sentences a cross-state paper exists to produce and exactly the sentences other authors will cite - contain at least one sign reversal, two misidentified exception states, one claim contradicted in four states, one Discussion claim contradicted by its own Results, several silently-truncated 'all states' universals, and a Conclusion that converts association into mechanism. Read the tables. Do not read only the prose.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Strong (high confidence)

This is the first study to apply harmonized variable definitions, sample rules, and models to special education teacher (SET) workforce data from seven state longitudinal data systems simultaneously, and its central contribution is measurement infrastructure as much as substance: it removes (partially) the methodological confound that has made prior single-state SET findings incommensurable. Several substantive findings are genuinely new to the SET literature -- large certification deficits in special education schools in every state, charter-sector SET staffing gaps, quantified switching-to-general-education flows, and dramatic cross-state heterogeneity in the certification-turnover association -- while others confirm well-established patterns. The paper's most quotable lines (turnover of 'nearly half the workforce,' and the conclusion that turnover gaps by school poverty were 'likely driven by' inequitable SET distribution) run ahead of what its own tables report, and cross-state comparisons of levels are undercut by state-specific SET identification rules the authors themselves flag.

**Strengths:**

- The core contribution is real and durable: seven SLDSs analyzed with the same SET-identification protocol (>=50% of assignments or >=0.50 FTE), the same CEDS-aligned variable definitions where possible, the same within-state quartile constructions, and the same LPM specifications. Prior cross-state inference in this literature was impossible precisely because it could not separate genuine state differences from analyst choices (the authors' own Gilmour, Feng & Theobald 2025 makes this point). This paper is the first to hold the analytic choices fixed.
- Several findings are new to the SET literature rather than confirmatory. (a) SETs in special education schools were substantially less likely to be fully certified than SETs in traditional schools in all seven states, ranging from 6.7 to 73.5 percentage points (Table 3) -- a consistent, large, previously undocumented gap. (b) Turnover in special education schools is sharply heterogeneous across states (4.1-6.1 pp lower attrition in MA/TX/WA but 21.4 pp higher in VA, Table 4); the authors credibly claim this is the first examination of SET turnover by school type. (c) The charter sector is documented for SETs specifically: 22.6-40.5 pp higher novice probability (Table 1), lower certification (Table 3), and 7.4-25.8 pp higher attrition (Table 4).
- Switching to general education is treated as a first-class, quantified outflow rather than a footnote to attrition. The paper shows switching is a large share of total turnover in Indiana, Massachusetts, and Texas, and that full certification is associated with 3.7 to 40.3 pp lower switching probability (Table 5). This reframes 'SET shortage' as partly an internal reallocation problem, not only a profession-exit problem -- a policy-relevant distinction most single-state and national-survey work cannot make.
- The magnitude of cross-state heterogeneity in teacher-level associations is the paper's most useful and least-anticipated result. Full certification is associated with 18.8 pp lower attrition in Texas but only 2.4 pp in Virginia (Table 4); novices are 10.1 pp more likely to leave in Hawaii but 1.9 pp in Pennsylvania and not at all in Texas (Table 4). SETs of color have lower attrition in Hawaii and Texas but higher attrition in Indiana and Pennsylvania. This heterogeneity is a direct rebuke to the field's habit of generalizing one state's SET turnover findings nationally.
- The paper is unusually candid about the limits of its own cross-state comparisons. The Discussion explicitly names Indiana's setting-based and Texas's student-population-served identification rules as likely explanations for their low SET workforce shares and probable inflators of their switching rates, and concedes that experience and certification constructs 'were not comparable in practice.' Most papers with this much comparative real estate to defend would concede less.
- Strong open-science and follow-on infrastructure: OSF preregistration (with an explicit deviations section), full regression results posted, a public data explorer, and a companion methods paper (Gilmour et al. 2026, TESE) reporting sensitivity to SET identification and multi-school handling. This makes the paper usable as a platform rather than a one-off.
- It offers a useful nuance to the received wisdom that SETs turn over more than general educators: true in five of seven states, but not in Massachusetts or Pennsylvania, and the gap where it exists is modest (1.2 pp in Texas to 5.5 pp in Virginia). It also contradicts prior SASS-based findings on special education schools (Mason-Williams & Gagnon 2017), which is a genuine, well-flagged correction rather than an incidental discrepancy.

**Weaknesses:**

- The single most quotable sentence in the paper -- 'turnover of nearly half the workforce (which we found in one state and in some locations in other states) is clearly unsustainable' -- does not correspond to any number in the main text. The highest total turnover the paper reports is Texas at 35.9% in an average year; Pennsylvania is 16.8%. 'Nearly half' appears to come from a subgroup or a supplementary cell, but as written it reads as a state-level figure and will almost certainly be cited that way. Compounding this, 'total turnover' includes moving schools, which is a loss to a school but not to the state workforce; a policy brief quoting 'half the SET workforce leaves' would be conflating two very different things.
- The Conclusion escalates beyond the Results. The Discussion hedges appropriately -- descriptive within-state stability differences 'may be due to' unequal distribution of SET characteristics -- but the Conclusion asserts that higher turnover in schools serving marginalized students 'was likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs.' That is a mediation claim, and the supporting evidence is a model-building exercise reported only in prose ('the associations between SET characteristics and stability stayed substantively the same in most states after the addition of school and district characteristics'), with no sequential tables, decomposition, or formal mediation test in the article. An equally consistent reading is that certification and novice status proxy for unobserved school working conditions that drive both sorting and turnover, in which case the causal arrow is not the one the Conclusion implies.
- The compositional story is also less uniform than the Conclusion suggests. Attrition shows no association with school FRPL share in any of the seven states (Table 4), but switching and moving are positively associated with school poverty in four states (Tables 5-6). So 'composition explains the poverty gap' holds cleanly only for one of three turnover types; for the other two, a school-poverty association survives the teacher controls.
- Cross-state comparison of LEVELS -- the share of the teacher workforce that is SET (8.6% IN to 18.4% HI), certification rates, switching rates, attrition rates -- is the paper's most citable-looking output and its least defensible. States identify SETs through fundamentally different instruments (an indicator in HI, assignment codes in MA/PA/VA, student-population-served in TX, classroom setting in IN, a special-education funding code in WA), and these will differ systematically in how they treat part-time, dually assigned, and inclusion-setting staff. The authors say so; readers will still quote the numbers.
- Attrition is defined as absence from the state dataset the following year, so it bundles out-of-state migration, private-school moves, district-office roles (explicitly excluded from the sample), and non-district entities (Pennsylvania intermediate units, explicitly excluded). States differ enormously in border porousness and in how much of the SET workforce sits outside district payrolls -- Pennsylvania's IU exclusion is particularly consequential for the state the paper holds up as the low-turnover exemplar. Cross-state attrition levels therefore are not clean comparisons even setting SET identification aside.
- Indiana is not on the same footing as the other six states: its analytic sample runs only 2017-18 to 2019-20, so its stability estimates rest on roughly two transitions and are entirely pre-COVID, yet Indiana appears in every table beside states with six years spanning the pandemic. Any reader comparing Indiana's turnover levels or trends to Texas's or Virginia's is comparing different eras. The paper notes the data constraint in Methods but does not carry the caveat into the results narrative or the state-specific policy recommendations (including the Massachusetts/Indiana switching prescription).
- The paper's central claim -- that SET workforce challenges vary across states -- is asserted from side-by-side point estimates rather than tested. There is no pooled model with state interactions and no formal test that, say, Texas's -18.8 pp certification-attrition coefficient differs from Virginia's -2.4 pp. With seven states, six tables, and roughly 25 rows each, several hundred coefficients are evaluated at p<=.05 with no multiple-comparison adjustment, and the narrative selects patterns from that space. The largest contrasts are surely real; the smaller ones the paper narrates as cross-state differences (e.g., 1.4 vs 1.5 vs 5.5 pp novice-by-middle-school differences) are not established.
- The novice indicator is constructed from data entry in the three excluded lead-in years rather than observed, and the authors note it miscodes re-entrants as novices. Novice status carries a large share of the paper's story, and the miscoding rate will differ across states with different re-entry patterns and different data histories -- another channel by which apparent cross-state heterogeneity could be measurement.
- The paper diagnoses variation without explaining it. Speculative explanations in the Discussion (Hawaii's island geography, Indiana's private-school options, differing certification requirements, compensation and retirement packages) are offered untested. The headline policy inference -- that interventions should be state-specific -- follows only weakly from the finding that outcomes vary by state; variation in symptoms does not by itself imply variation in effective treatments. That inference is the paper's most-quoted conclusion and is the part with the least direct evidentiary support.
- The state-specific policy prescriptions rest on the paper's most selection-prone coefficients. The Texas recommendation (certification fee waivers under HB 2) is grounded in the very large Texas certification coefficients (-18.8 pp attrition, -31.1 pp switching), but these are cross-sectional associations in which certification status is plainly endogenous: teachers intending to stay invest in certification, and emergency-permit hires are marginal entrants for reasons unrelated to the permit. Texas is also the state whose SET identification rule the authors say may inflate switching, so the two coefficients driving the recommendation are the two most vulnerable to the state's own definitional artifact.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the existence and rough magnitude of cross-state heterogeneity in SET workforce composition, distribution, and stability. This is now the best available evidence for 'SET staffing challenges look different in different states' and should displace the practice of generalizing a single state's SET turnover estimate nationally.
- CITE IT FOR: within-state associations between teacher characteristics and turnover -- novice status and full certification predict attrition, switching, and moving in most states, and teacher characteristics dominate school and district characteristics (school/district student-composition coefficients are only ~0.5-1.5 pp per SD). These are the paper's most robust estimates because they are internal to each state's data and do not depend on cross-state definitional comparability.
- CITE IT FOR: the certification deficit in special education schools -- lower full certification in all seven states, 6.7 to 73.5 pp. This is new, consistent across every state, and the single finding least vulnerable to the paper's measurement caveats since it is a within-state, within-year school-type contrast.
- CITE IT FOR: SET staffing in the charter sector (higher novice share, lower certification, higher attrition than traditional public schools in states with charter sectors). Reason: this is close to the only SET-specific charter evidence at scale, and it aligns with general-education charter findings (Weis et al. 2024), which raises confidence.
- CITE IT FOR: switching to general education as a quantitatively important, separately measurable outflow -- and for the point that its share of turnover varies substantially by state. Prior SET turnover work often collapses this into attrition.
- CITE IT FOR: the corrective that SET attrition exceeds general-educator attrition in most but not all states, and by modest margins (1.2-5.5 pp), rather than the blanket claim that SETs leave at much higher rates.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the claim that any state loses 'nearly half' its SET workforce annually. Reason: the paper's own reported maximum is Texas at 35.9% total turnover in an average year, and total turnover includes school moves, which are not workforce exits. Quote 35.9% (TX) and 16.8% (PA) instead.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the causal claim that inequitable SET distribution 'drives' higher turnover in schools serving marginalized students. Reason: the supporting model-building is described only in prose with no sequential tables or mediation test, and controlling for certification and novice status may simply be conditioning on a proxy for the unobserved working conditions that produce both the sorting and the turnover.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: cross-state rankings of SET share of the workforce, certification rates, switching rates, or attrition levels. Reason: each state identifies SETs with a different instrument (indicator, assignment code, student population served, classroom setting, funding code), and the authors themselves attribute Indiana's and Texas's low workforce shares -- and Texas's high switching -- to those rules rather than to real differences.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: Pennsylvania as a low-turnover benchmark without caveat. Reason: the sample excludes SETs employed by intermediate units, a structurally significant part of Pennsylvania's SET workforce, so the state's favorable numbers are partly a sample-construction artifact.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: Indiana comparisons on turnover levels, time trends, or COVID-era effects. Reason: Indiana's analytic window is 2017-18 to 2019-20 only, entirely pre-pandemic and roughly two transitions, while the other states span 2017-18 to 2022-23.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: certification as a causal lever for retention, or as an evaluation of certification-fee or licensure policy. Reason: the certification-turnover coefficients are cross-sectional associations with obvious selection (retention-minded teachers invest in certification; emergency-permit holders are a selected marginal-entrant population), and the largest of them sit in the state whose SET-identification rule the authors flag as potentially inflating switching.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: claims that a specific cross-state difference in a coefficient is statistically distinguishable. Reason: the paper estimates each state separately and never formally tests cross-state differences; readers should treat only the very large contrasts (e.g., 18.8 vs 2.4 pp on certification-attrition) as established heterogeneity.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: national estimates or generalization beyond the seven states. Reason: the states are the ones the IES-funded center could obtain data from, not a designed sample; no California, Florida, New York, or Deep South state is included. To the paper's credit, it never claims national representativeness -- readers, not the authors, are the risk here.
- OPEN QUESTION: why states differ. The paper documents heterogeneity but offers only untested speculation (geography, private-school competition, certification requirements, compensation, service-delivery models). Nothing here identifies which state policies or structures produce which workforce patterns.
- OPEN QUESTION: what any of this means for students. The paper explicitly does not link SET composition, distribution, or stability to student outcomes, and cites only external evidence (Kaler et al. 2025 in Washington) that SET turnover harms achievement for students with disabilities. Do not use this paper to quantify the student cost of SET instability.
- OPEN QUESTION: how much of the cross-state variation is measurement versus reality. The companion methods paper (Gilmour et al. 2026, Teacher Education and Special Education) reports sensitivity to SET-identification and multi-school choices, and should be read alongside this one before citing any cross-state level comparison. The OSF materials (https://osf.io/qkpnz/) hold the full regression output the article omits.
- OPEN QUESTION: whether the special education school certification gap and the charter-sector gaps reflect different labor supply, different regulatory exposure, or different demand -- and whether the sharply divergent special-education-school turnover (Virginia +21.4 pp attrition vs Texas and Washington lower) reflects different institutional definitions of 'special education school' across states.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW. It is worth separating the two contributions this paper makes, because they have different strengths and will be cited for different things. The first is infrastructural: seven state longitudinal data systems analyzed with a common SET-identification protocol, common CEDS-aligned variable definitions, common within-state quartile constructions, and identical LPM specifications, with preregistration, posted regression output, a public data explorer, and a companion methods paper on identification sensitivity. This is the contribution that will still matter in ten years. The field's prior state of knowledge was a set of single-state SLDS studies and national survey snapshots that could not be compared, a problem the authors diagnosed themselves in Gilmour, Feng & Theobald (2025). Holding the analytic choices fixed is genuinely the first step, and nobody had taken it.

The second contribution is substantive, and here the paper is a mix. A fair amount confirms what the field already believed: novice and uncertified SETs turn over more (Billingsley & Bettini 2019; Nguyen et al. 2020); charter schools employ less experienced, less certified staff (Weis et al. 2024); descriptive turnover gaps by school poverty attenuate or vanish once teacher characteristics are controlled (which the authors explicitly align with Pendola & Perrone 2025). None of that updates priors much, though the cross-state replication does convert 'probably true' into 'true in six or seven states.'

But several findings are new. The certification deficit in special education schools -- lower in all seven states, 6.7 to 73.5 percentage points (Table 3) -- had not been documented, and it contradicts prior SASS-based work finding no SET quality difference in special education schools (Mason-Williams & Gagnon 2017); the authors flag the contradiction rather than bury it. The turnover heterogeneity in special education schools (4.1-6.1 pp lower attrition in Massachusetts, Texas, and Washington but 21.4 pp higher in Virginia, Table 4) is, as the authors claim, apparently the first look at SET turnover by school type. Switching to general education gets treated as a first-class outflow with real magnitudes rather than as a residual, and full certification is associated with 3.7 to 40.3 pp lower switching (Table 5) -- reframing SET shortage as partly an internal reallocation problem. And the cross-state variation in the teacher-level coefficients themselves is the most interesting thing in the paper: full certification predicts 18.8 pp lower attrition in Texas but 2.4 pp in Virginia; novices are 10.1 pp more likely to leave in Hawaii, 1.9 pp in Pennsylvania, and not at all in Texas (where the coefficient is -0.0015 and insignificant). That last pattern is a direct challenge to the field's habit of importing one state's SET retention estimate as a general fact.

QUOTABLE VERSUS SUPPORTED. Two gaps deserve flagging, because both will be exploited in citation. The first is the Discussion's line that 'turnover of nearly half the workforce (which we found in one state and in some locations in other states) is clearly unsustainable.' The highest figure the article actually reports is Texas at 35.9% total turnover in an average year. 'Nearly half' does not appear in any table or in the results narrative; it presumably comes from a subgroup cell in Figure 5 or the supplementary appendix, neither of which is verifiable in the text as extracted. But the phrasing -- 'in one state' -- reads as a state-level rate, and it is a near-certainty that policy briefs will quote it as one. The problem compounds because 'total turnover' bundles school moves with exits: a SET who transfers between two schools in the same district is counted, and that is a real disruption to a school but not a loss to the state workforce. Readers should use the state total-turnover figures the paper does report (35.9% Texas, 16.8% Pennsylvania) and should say explicitly what those include.

The second gap is the Conclusion's assertion that 'higher turnover in schools serving more marginalized student populations was likely driven by the inequitable distribution of fully certified, experienced SETs across settings.' This is a mediation claim, and the paper does not run a mediation analysis. Its support is: descriptive gaps exist (Figure 5), those gaps are 'seldom and inconsistently evident' in the regressions once teacher characteristics enter, and a model-building exercise described in a single prose sentence found the SET-characteristic coefficients stable as school and district controls were added. That is consistent with the claim but does not establish it. A competing explanation the paper cannot rule out is that certification and novice status are proxies for unobserved school working conditions that produce both the sorting of less-qualified SETs into these schools and their elevated turnover; controlling for the proxy would attenuate the school-poverty coefficient without the causal story being right. Notably, the Discussion hedges correctly ('may be due to') and the Conclusion does not ('was likely driven by') -- a within-paper escalation readers should notice, since the Conclusion sentence is the one that gets quoted. It is also worth noting the pattern is not uniform across turnover types: attrition shows no FRPL association in any state (Table 4), but switching and moving retain positive school-poverty associations in four states (Tables 5-6), so the compositional explanation is clean for only one of the three outcomes.

LEVELS VERSUS ASSOCIATIONS. This is the most important thing for a reader to internalize about how to use the paper. The within-state associations -- who turns over, which school types employ which SETs, how the certification gradient operates inside a given state -- are robust, because they are internal to a single state's data and do not depend on whether Texas and Hawaii count SETs the same way. The cross-state comparisons of levels are much weaker, because they depend on exactly that. Hawaii uses a SET indicator; Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia use assignment codes; Texas uses an indicator for student population served; Indiana uses classroom setting; Washington uses a special-education funding code. These instruments will differ systematically in whether they capture inclusion-setting teachers, part-time and dually assigned staff, and paraprofessional-adjacent roles, and the >=50%/>=0.50 FTE rule interacts with each differently. The authors are commendably direct about this: they name Indiana's and Texas's rules as likely explanations for those states' low SET workforce shares, and note that Texas's rule 'may have conflated SETs and general educators ... potentially inflated estimates of the rates of switching.' There is a tension the paper does not fully resolve, though, in that it then builds state-specific policy recommendations partly on these levels -- most conspicuously the Texas recommendation, which rests on the two Texas certification coefficients (-18.8 pp attrition, -31.1 pp switching) that are largest precisely in the state whose definitional artifact the authors flag.

Attrition has a parallel problem. It is defined as absence from the state dataset next year, so it absorbs out-of-state migration, private-school employment, district-office roles (excluded from the sample by design), and non-district entities (Pennsylvania's intermediate units, also excluded). States differ in border porousness and in how much of the SET workforce sits outside district payrolls. Pennsylvania's IU exclusion matters most here, since Pennsylvania is the state the paper repeatedly holds up as the low-turnover contrast case.

COMPARABILITY ACROSS STATES, MORE GENERALLY. Two further asymmetries limit how much weight the cross-state frame can bear. Indiana's analytic sample runs only 2017-18 to 2019-20 -- pre-pandemic, roughly two transitions -- while every other state spans six years including COVID. Indiana nonetheless appears in every table beside those states, and the Massachusetts/Indiana switching recommendation is built on it. And the novice indicator is constructed from entry into the data in the three excluded lead-in years, which the authors note miscodes re-entrants; the miscoding rate will vary across states with different re-entry patterns, which means some of the apparent cross-state heterogeneity in novice coefficients could be measurement rather than labor markets.

Finally, the paper's central claim -- heterogeneity across states -- is never formally tested. Each state is estimated separately and the differences are read off side-by-side point estimates. There is no pooled model with state interactions, no test that Texas's certification coefficient differs from Virginia's, and no multiple-comparison adjustment across what amounts to several hundred coefficients evaluated at p<=.05. The very large contrasts are surely real. The smaller ones the narrative treats as cross-state differences (the 1.4 / 1.5 / 5.5 pp novice-by-middle-school comparisons, for instance) are not established, and readers should not cite them as such.

GENERALIZABILITY AND BOUNDARIES. Seven states, selected by data availability through an IES-funded center rather than by design. They are reasonably diverse in structure and geography -- Hawaii is a single statewide district, Texas is large and decentralized, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania are northeastern, Virginia and Washington and Indiana fill in -- but there is no California, Florida, New York, or Deep South state. To the paper's credit, it never claims national representativeness and consistently frames results as state-specific; the boundaries are drawn honestly. What is missing is any characterization of how these seven compare to national benchmarks on shortage severity or SET workforce structure, which would let a reader judge whether the sample is unusually troubled or unusually calm. The generalization risk sits with citers, not with the authors.

STANDING AND FOLLOW-ON. Notwithstanding all of the above, this is now the best available evidence on its question, and by a wide margin, because the realistic alternatives are worse: national surveys with small SET subsamples, self-report, and no longitudinal turnover decomposition; or single-state studies that are not comparable to each other. Nothing else exists at this scale with harmonized definitions. It should become the default citation for the proposition that SET workforce challenges vary substantially by state and that uniform national policy responses are poorly matched to that variation -- a claim supported at the level of pattern even where individual magnitudes are shaky.

The follow-on agenda the paper sets up is unusually concrete: the companion methods paper on SET identification (Gilmour et al. 2026), the public data explorer, and explicit calls for work on student outcomes, on service-delivery models as an explanation for the SET-share variation, on the charter sector, on special education schools, and on evaluating state policy responses (Texas HB 2; Hawaii's differential compensation, already studied in Theobald et al. 2025). The most important unresolved item is causal: the paper diagnoses variation richly and explains none of it. Its policy inference -- that interventions should be state-specific -- is a reasonable but untested step from 'outcomes vary by state' to 'effective treatments vary by state,' and it is worth being explicit that the paper's headline policy conclusion is an inference rather than a finding.

RATING. Strong. The infrastructure contribution is real and reusable, multiple substantive findings are new to the SET literature, the paper is candid about its measurement limits to an unusual degree, and it becomes the reference work on its question by default. The weaknesses are about how it will be cited -- levels mistaken for comparable, a mediation claim asserted more confidently in the Conclusion than the Results support, and a 'nearly half' figure that overshoots the paper's own maximum -- rather than about whether the paper earns its place. Confidence 0.85: I have the full article text, but figures, supplementary appendices, and the OSF materials were unavailable, which limits verification of the 'nearly half' figure, the model-building results, and the descriptive turnover distributions in Figure 5.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

For a seven-state study built on restricted state longitudinal data systems, the open-science scaffolding is unusually good: a dated Center for Open Science preregistration, an OSF project holding code, supplemental materials, and full regression output, a dedicated "Deviations from Preregistration" section, a public data explorer, and a Method section that documents most sample and variable construction in real detail. What is missing is the journal-era baseline that would let a reader act on any of it: there is no data availability statement, no described access pathway for the seven state agreements beyond an Acknowledgments list of agencies, several discretionary sample exclusions are unquantified, and a number of reported quantities in the tables (notably the shifting Ns across Tables 4-6) are never explained. Readers can independently verify essentially none of the state-level estimates and should treat the cross-state level comparisons in particular as contingent on definitional choices whose defense is offloaded to a companion paper.

**Strengths:**

- Preregistered with the Center for Open Science on a stated date (October 3, 2024) with a live OSF project (https://osf.io/qkpnz/) said to hold the preregistration, code, and supplemental materials — considerably more than the modal administrative-data education paper.
- A dedicated "Deviations from Preregistration" section that names the deviations (analytic window, exclusion of SETs not linked to schools, school-count rather than FTE weighting, novice constructed from the data, dropping school-level English learner share, adding school type, collapsing within- and cross-district moves, LPM rather than discrete-time hazard models) and gives a reason for each. Disclosed deviation is far more useful to a reader than silent conformity.
- Full regression output — including the outcomes (advanced degree, gender) and the coefficients (school and district percent AIAN, AAPI, NHPI, two-or-more-races) suppressed from the main tables — is stated to be deposited on OSF rather than "available on request," and table notes explicitly enumerate which controls are in the model but not shown.
- Variable construction is documented at an unusual level of granularity for a seven-state harmonization: the two-stage SET rule (>=50% of assignments or >=0.50 FTE teaching, then the same threshold within special education), the 1/(number of schools) weighting for multi-school SETs, the inclusion-only-in-SET-years rule, the four mutually exclusive turnover categories with the switching-dominates-moving tiebreak, the CEDS alignment for experience and full certification, and the within-state (and within-state-by-year, for continuous measures) standardization/quartile scheme.
- Sources of every non-SLDS covariate are named and are themselves public: CCD via ElSi for school and district characteristics, Massachusetts DESE for economic disadvantage in place of FRPL, Ed Data Express for English learner shares in 2020-21 and 2021-22, IDEA 618 for the students-with-disabilities-per-SET ratios in Figure 1. The entire school/district side of the panel is therefore rebuildable by anyone.
- Missingness in covariates is quantified rather than glossed (12.3% of school-year and 71.9% of district-year observations missing at least one variable) and the imputation rule (carry forward the most recent nonmissing year) is stated, along with the specific variables driving it (English learner and IEP district variables in the CCD).
- Software is named (Stata), the significance threshold is stated, the estimating equations name their year effects and SET-level clustering, and a public data explorer (sparccenter.org) exposes the composition-over-time results outside the article.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement. The article carries Funding, Conflicts, ORCID, and a one-line "Supplemental material ... is available online" note, but nothing that tells a replicator whether the seven SLDS extracts can be obtained, under what instrument, from whom, or on what timeline. The Acknowledgments name the seven state agencies, which is the closest thing to a contact list, and the Method says data-sharing agreements did not include student-level data in every state — but there is no description of the agreements, no citation of a DUA process or restricted-use application, and no statement of whether the authors can broker access. A would-be replicator must reconstruct seven separate negotiations from scratch with no guidance.
- Two of the most consequential design choices — how SETs are identified in each state, and how multi-school SETs are handled — are defended not in this article but by pointing to a companion paper (Gilmour et al., 2026, TESE) with "reported elsewhere" and "substantively similar results." Since the paper's own Discussion concedes that the cross-state spread in the SET share of the workforce (8.6% in Indiana vs. 18.4% in Hawaii) "could be an artifact of variability in data-collection practices," the sensitivity evidence that would bound that artifact is not in the paper a reader is holding.
- Discretionary exclusions are unquantified. "In Massachusetts and Indiana, we excluded districts that did not report any SETs in some years, which suggested reporting errors" gives no district list, no count, no share of the sample lost, and no rule (how many zero-report years triggered exclusion; whether the district was dropped in all years or only the affected years). The same applies to the exclusion of district-only SETs and cross-district entities such as Pennsylvania intermediate units: acknowledged in Limitations, never sized.
- Several Ns are unexplained and at least one set is internally puzzling. Tables 1-3 use identical samples within each state, so Virginia's drop from 108,623 (novice, certification) to 87,217 (SET of color) evidently reflects dropping the 18.8% with missing race/ethnicity when race is the outcome rather than a covariate — sensible, but a reader has to reverse-engineer it. Tables 4-6 are worse: three mutually exclusive turnover outcomes estimated on what is described as one base sample return different and non-monotonic Ns (Hawaii 11,369 / 10,346 / 10,250; Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361; Pennsylvania 108,904 / 106,206 / 110,408). Nothing in the text explains whether switching and moving are estimated conditional on not leaving, whether outcome missingness differs, or whether some other restriction applies — and the Texas pattern is inconsistent with a simple nested-conditioning story. The estimand for switching and moving is therefore ambiguous as reported.
- It is never stated whether the 1/(number of schools) weights are carried into the regressions, and if so under what Stata weight type. The weighting is introduced as a sample-inclusion and stability-outcome device; whether Equations (1) and (2) are weighted materially affects the coefficients, the standard errors, and the interpretation of the reported Ns (which appear to be observation counts, not weighted counts).
- The imputation rule is underspecified for a case that must arise often given 71.9% district-year missingness: what happens when there is no earlier nonmissing year (backward fill, drop, or something else), and whether carry-forward is applied before or after the within-state-by-year standardization — which matters, because a carried-forward raw value standardized against a later year's distribution is a different variable from a carried-forward standardized value.
- The English learner measure changes source mid-panel (CCD district data for 2017-18 through 2019-20, Ed Data Express for 2020-21 and 2021-22) and no source is named for 2022-23, the last analytic year. A measurement break that coincides with the pandemic years, absorbed into common year effects, is a live threat to the several English-learner coefficients the Results lean on, and the article gives a reader no way to gauge it.
- Massachusetts's poverty measure is DESE economic disadvantage, not FRPL, yet the table rows and notes label it "School % FRPL" / "District % FRPL" uniformly across all seven states. A reader comparing the Massachusetts poverty coefficients to the others is comparing different constructs under one label.
- Reporting is thin on everything except point estimates: coefficients, standard errors, stars, and Ns, with no confidence intervals, no R-squared or any fit statistic (a gap the paper itself names as a motivation for the supplemental logits), no outcome means or descriptive tables for the regression samples (composition and turnover levels appear only in figures whose underlying numbers are not tabulated in the article), and no ICC values in the main tables despite ICCs being described in the Analysis and interpreted in the Results.
- The "model building" result that anchors one of the Discussion's headline interpretations — that the SET-of-color/stability associations in Indiana and Pennsylvania "declined in magnitude by nearly half after the addition of school characteristics" — appears in prose only, with no numbers, no table, and no place in the Supplemental Analyses list (which covers logits, specified urbanicity categories, hazard models, and general-educator descriptives). Unlike the logit and hazard results, this one is not even promised on OSF.
- The novice construction has an unresolved edge: inexperience is defined from first appearance in the three pre-analytic years "in most cases, 2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17," but Indiana's analytic sample runs only 2017-18 to 2019-20 "due to data-collection constraints," and the article never says which states departed from the standard lookback or whether Indiana had a comparable pre-period. Left-censoring (SETs already present in the first observed year) is not discussed at all, and the article acknowledges but does not bound the reentrant-miscoded-as-novice problem.
- The article's central methodological claim is that analyzing seven states "in the same way" separates real variation from methodological variation, yet it never documents how identical code was executed across seven separate restricted environments — whether one codebase ran in all seven, who executed it, and how output was validated. That process documentation is exactly what would substantiate the harmonization claim, and it is absent from the article.
- No Stata version, package list, or seed is reported, and there is no indication whether the posted code is runnable against synthetic or example data or is a set of do-files inert without seven DUAs.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before leaning on any state-level estimate, go to https://osf.io/qkpnz/ first and check three things: (a) whether the preregistration's original specifications match what the Deviations section reports, (b) whether the posted code includes the sample-construction steps (the Massachusetts/Indiana district exclusions, the carry-forward imputation, the multi-school weighting) or only the estimation step, and (c) whether the full regression output tables report the Ns and the weight statement that the article omits. If the posted material is estimation-only, the sample-construction guesses listed below remain guesses.
- Treat the cross-state comparison of SET workforce share (Figure 1, top panel) as the least portable finding in the paper. The authors themselves flag it as possibly an artifact of how each SLDS identifies SETs — Indiana by classroom setting and Texas by student population served, versus explicit indicators or assignment codes elsewhere. Read Gilmour et al. (2026), Teacher Education and Special Education 49(1), which carries the sensitivity analyses on SET identification and multi-school handling, before citing any cross-state level difference; this article reports only that alternatives were "substantively similar" without showing them.
- Ask the authors (or check the OSF output) for the Ns and estimation samples behind Tables 4-6. Three mutually exclusive outcomes returning different, non-monotonic Ns within the same state means the denominators differ, and the interpretation of the switching and moving coefficients depends entirely on whether leavers are in or out of those samples. Until that is resolved, read the attrition results (Table 4) as the cleanest of the three and the switching/moving results as conditional on an unstated restriction.
- Do not read the Massachusetts "% FRPL" coefficients as comparable to the other states'; that column is DESE economic disadvantage. If a cross-state poverty comparison matters for your purposes, rebuild the poverty measure yourself from CCD/ElSi for all seven states — those data are public — and ask whether the Massachusetts contrast survives.
- Discount the English-learner coefficients relative to the other covariates. The measure switches from CCD to Ed Data Express between 2019-20 and 2020-21, has no stated source for 2022-23, and sits inside the variable set responsible for the 71.9% district-year carry-forward. The several English-learner findings in the Results and Discussion are the ones most likely to move under a consistent measure.
- Ask specifically how many districts and district-years were dropped in Massachusetts and Indiana under the zero-SET-reporting rule, and what share of each state's SETs that represents. Indiana's analytic sample is already the smallest and shortest (2017-18 to 2019-20, N ~ 12,500-17,400 depending on the table), so an unquantified district-level exclusion there is proportionally the most consequential in the study.
- Treat the charter school findings as exploratory rather than confirmatory. School type is an explicit addition to the analytic plan after preregistration, and the charter coefficients are among the largest in the paper (22.6 to 40.5 percentage points on novice status; 7.4 to 25.8 on attrition). They are interesting and consistent across states, but they carry none of the preregistration's discipline and no correction for the number of school-type contrasts estimated.
- Do not cite the "coefficient falls by half with school controls" claim for Indiana and Pennsylvania SETs of color without asking for the numbers. It is prose-only, is not in the enumerated supplemental analyses, and is load-bearing for the Discussion's central interpretive move (that within-state stability differences reflect unequal distribution of SET characteristics rather than school effects).
- What you can verify without any data agreement: every covariate on the school and district side (CCD/ElSi enrollment, locale, race/ethnicity shares, school type and level; DESE economic disadvantage; Ed Data Express EL shares), the within-state quartile cutpoints those imply, and the IDEA 618 students-with-disabilities-per-SET denominators in Figure 1's bottom panel.
