The composition-over-time results also have a second public expression in the sparccenter.org data explorer, which is worth cross-checking against Figures 2 and 3.
- What is effectively unverifiable without all seven DUAs: every SET-level quantity in the paper — the composition percentages, all certification and race/ethnicity distributions, every turnover rate, and every coefficient in Tables 1-6. There is no partial path (no public microdata, no synthetic sample described in the article), and reconstruction would require negotiating separately with seven state agencies whose agreements are not described. Plan on treating these as authoritative-but-uncheckable descriptive estimates rather than as replicable results.
- If you intend an actual replication, budget for the choices you will have to make blind: whether regressions are weighted by 1/(number of schools) and with which Stata weight type; whether the >=50%/>=0.50 FTE special education threshold is taken over all assignments or only teaching assignments; what the imputation does when no prior nonmissing year exists; whether quartiles are cut pooled across years or within state-by-year; and how ties are resolved in the overlapping grade-span definitions of elementary/middle/high. Each is a fork the article does not close, and the first two could move coefficients materially.
- Read the Deviations section as a strength, but note which deviation matters most for interpretation rather than replication: abandoning discrete-time hazard models for LPMs in the stability analyses. The stated reason (sample loss from following teachers over time, plus unreliable experience data) is credible, but it means the headline stability estimates are pooled year-to-year transition probabilities rather than duration models. The hazard-model results exist only on OSF; if career trajectories rather than annual transitions are your question, those supplemental results, not Tables 4-6, are the relevant exhibit.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Judged against the realistic ceiling for a study that pools seven separately negotiated state longitudinal data systems, this paper is at the upper end of current practice — but the gap between its open-science gestures and its actionable documentation is wide enough that a reader should calibrate carefully about what is checkable.

On the credit side, the infrastructure is real and dated. The Method opens by naming a Center for Open Science preregistration (October 3, 2024) and an OSF project holding preregistration, code, and supplemental materials; the Results direct readers there for full regression output; supplemental analyses (logits replacing the LPMs, specified urbanicity categories, discrete-time hazard models for early-career SETs, general-educator descriptives) are said to live there too. A public data explorer at sparccenter.org gives the composition results a second, independent public expression. Most importantly, there is a dedicated Deviations from Preregistration section that is specific about what changed and why — the analytic window, the school-linkage restriction, school-count rather than FTE weighting, novice constructed from data rather than the SLDS experience field, dropping school-level English learner share because the CCD does not carry it, adding school type, collapsing within- and cross-district moves, and substituting LPMs for the preregistered hazard models. Deposited output beats "available on request," and disclosed deviation beats silence; both should be credited.

On the debit side, the single most consequential omission is the absence of a data availability statement. The article carries the standard AERJ apparatus — Acknowledgments, ORCID iDs, Funding (IES Grant R324C240002), Conflicts, a one-line supplemental-material note — but nothing that tells a replicator how the seven SLDS extracts were obtained or could be obtained again. The Acknowledgments thank the Hawaii DOE, Indiana DOE, Massachusetts DESE, Pennsylvania DOE, Texas Education Agency, Virginia DOE, and Washington OSPI, which at least identifies whom to approach, and the Method notes in passing that data-sharing agreements did not include student-level data in every state. That is the whole of it: no description of the instruments, no application process, no timeline, no statement of whether the authors can facilitate access, no per-state pointer beyond "see the Supplementary Materials for more information about each state." For a paper whose contribution is precisely the assembly of these seven systems, the assembly is the least documented part.

Sample construction is the paper's strongest documentation and still leaves a replicator with several blind forks. The SET identification rule is stated twice over (teacher if >=50% of assignments or >=0.50 FTE are teaching; SET if >=50% of assignments or >=0.50 FTE are special education), but the denominator for the second test is not pinned down, and the "or" leaves which criterion binds in which state to Appendix Table A1. The multi-school weighting rule (1/number of schools) is clear as a concept, but the article never says whether those weights enter the regressions, which Stata weight type is used, or whether the reported Ns are observations or weighted counts — and that ambiguity propagates into the standard errors, which are otherwise well specified (clustered by SET). The exclusion of Massachusetts and Indiana districts that reported no SETs in some years is a genuinely discretionary judgment call reported without a rule, a count, or a share; Indiana's sample is the study's smallest and shortest window (2017-18 to 2019-20), so an unsized exclusion there is proportionally most consequential. The novice measure — first appearance in the pre-analytic window, "in most cases" 2014-15 through 2016-17 — never says which states departed from that window or how Indiana's shortened panel accommodated a lookback, and left-censoring goes unmentioned entirely. Finally, the covariate imputation is quantified honestly (12.3% of school-years, 71.9% of district-years missing at least one variable, filled by carry-forward) but underspecified operationally: nothing on what happens with no prior nonmissing year, and nothing on whether the fill precedes or follows the within-state-by-year standardization, which changes what the standardized variable means.

Specification transparency is adequate in substance and thin in reporting. Equations (1) and (2) are recoverable from prose: LPMs, school and district covariate vectors, teacher attributes added in the stability models, year effects, SEs clustered by SET, and the reason for LPM over logit (interpretability plus von Hippel's argument for non-rare events). The table notes do the right thing in enumerating suppressed controls (school and district AIAN, AAPI, NHPI, two-or-more-races shares; year fixed effects; plus pre-K and CTE in Tables 4-6). But advanced degree — available in four states and treated as an outcome in the distribution analyses — never appears as a control in the stability tables or in their notes, so whether it is in Equation (2) is simply unknown; the missing-data indicators (Virginia race/ethnicity, Indiana gender) are described in the Variables section and then vanish from tables and notes; and the omitted percent-White reference is never named. Reporting is coefficients, SEs, stars and Ns and nothing else: no confidence intervals, no fit statistic of any kind (the paper cites limited fit information as a motivation for the supplemental logits but never reports it), no outcome means for any regression sample, no tabulated numbers behind Figures 1-5, and no ICC values in the main tables despite ICCs being estimated, described in the Analysis section, and interpreted in the Results.

The Ns deserve particular attention because they are the one place the article's own numbers raise a question it never answers. Tables 1-3 report identical Ns within each state across all three outcomes (Hawaii 12,496; Indiana 17,423; Massachusetts 62,842; Pennsylvania 122,487; Texas 285,766; Washington 40,903), with the single exception of Virginia, whose N falls from 108,623 to 87,217 for the SET-of-color outcome — consistent with dropping the 18.8% with missing race when race is the dependent variable, but a reader has to work that out unaided. Tables 4-6, however, report three different Ns per state for three mutually exclusive turnover outcomes drawn from what is described as a single base sample, and the differences are not monotonic: Hawaii 11,369 / 10,346 / 10,250, Pennsylvania 108,904 / 106,206 / 110,408, Texas 214,889 / 227,484 / 208,361. A nested-conditioning design (switching estimated among non-leavers, moving among stayers-in-special-education) would explain the Hawaii ordering but is contradicted by Texas, where the switching sample exceeds the attrition sample. Whatever the explanation, the article does not give it, and without it the estimand behind the switching and moving coefficients — the population over which those probabilities are defined — is ambiguous. That ambiguity sits directly under one of the paper's policy conclusions, the high switching rates in Massachusetts, Indiana, and Texas.

Two further items are delegated in ways worth naming. First, the robustness of the two most consequential definitional choices — SET identification and multi-school handling — is not shown here at all but attributed to a companion paper (Gilmour et al., 2026, TESE 49(1)) with the phrase "substantively similar results." Given that the Discussion itself concedes the cross-state spread in SET workforce share may be a data-collection artifact, the evidence that would bound that artifact is one citation away rather than in hand. Second, the model-building result cited in the Discussion — SET-of-color stability coefficients in Indiana and Pennsylvania falling by nearly half once school characteristics enter — is prose-only, carries no numbers, and is not among the supplemental analyses the Method promises on OSF. It is load-bearing for the paper's central interpretation (that within-state stability gaps reflect the unequal distribution of SET characteristics rather than school effects per se), and it is the least verifiable claim in the article.

Finally, a structural point about what "reproducible" would even mean here. The paper's methodological contribution is that seven states were analyzed "in the same way," which is what licenses the inference that cross-state differences are real rather than methodological. Substantiating that claim requires documenting that a single codebase was executed in seven separate secure environments, by whom, with what validation of output — and the article contains none of that process documentation. The posted code may well settle it, but the article does not say so, and a reader who cannot reach the OSF project has no basis for the harmonization claim beyond the authors' assurance.

Net: readers should treat the school- and district-side data as fully public and reconstructible, the composition trends as cross-checkable against the public data explorer and IDEA 618, and every SET-level estimate — which is to say the entire empirical payload — as authoritative but effectively uncheckable without seven separate data agreements the article does not describe how to obtain.
